en: From the *Record of Probing the Elephant in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, as stated in the sūtra itself: there was a group of blind people who each felt an elephant with their hands. Those who felt the trunk said, "The elephant is like a winnowing basket.
Those who felt the thighs said, "The elephant is like a pillar. Those who felt the tail said, "The elephant is like a broom. Those who felt the belly...
Regarding the elephant, when it was like a stone, they said so; yet when one touched its eye, they said it was like a drum; when touching its ear, they said it was like an inverted hanging leaf;

and when touching its hoof, they said it was like an overturned cup on the ground. Those who held their respective perceptions disputed with one another, leaving onlookers to laugh until their bellies ached.

How is this different from those who discourse on the sutras today? Since the Buddha has already entered nirvana, there is no way to consult him; thus, people merely express their own subjective sentiments.
Using their hands as instruments of perception, they grope for one another’s features, standing like blind men criticizing the blind; I am truly grieved by this.
Knowing that we are all likewise blind, I consider it urgent to remedy this failing. Thus, I entered the ranks of the blind and grope along with the multitude.

Yet, regarding the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* among all the scriptures, there are even more points of doubt and contention. Consequently, these blind men clamor together, jostling arm-to-arm and pointing finger-to-finger, such that no resolution can be reached.
Who has here selected more than one hundred passages from this scripture and briefly analyzed them to serve as examples for the entire volume?

Furthermore, I have appended one or two [passages] from other scriptures without citing them at length. Formerly, when the disciples of the Buddha each set forth their own views, the Buddha told the assembly:
"What you all have said is not my intention; yet, as each of your words accords with principle and is sufficient to benefit sentient beings," then those...

One should examine the multitude [of interpretations] while setting aside those that contradict reason; by examining through reason, although one may not grasp the specific image, it is never the case that it is not the image.

Therefore, do not worry about "grasping" (the image); rather, clinging to [one's own view] as the truth is what is worrisome. If one leaves the mind empty, does not prioritize what was first encountered, and harmonizes the phrasing with the underlying principle—so that the principle accords with the text and the text flows smoothly—the intended meaning will manifest of itself.
As for the manifestation of the image, it leaps forth and stands out clearly; it is not something to be found apart from the act of grasping.
One elephant is like one who, grasping at what he feels against a solid wall, holds fast to it; the more diligently he feels for it, the further away he loses it.
This merely increases conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and results in the fault of slandering the Dharma—what benefit is there in this? This is specifically regarding matters of instruction;

however, those who discuss meditation (*dhyāna*) grasp even more excessively. Some grasp at a horse and claim it is an elephant; some grasp at emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and claim it is an elephant; and some...
"Feeling with the hands" means that although one perceives everything as being an elephant, or feels all over it and finds nothing, yet cannot say there is no elephant;
such various conflicting views are difficult to resolve even if one were to change the attendants. I pray that you, O virtuous ones, will instead feel for your own eyes;
once you have obtained the faculty of sight, there will be no need to feel for the elephant.
Written by the junior monk Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple on the Day of the Thousand Buddhas’ Bathing, in the year Renyin, the thirtieth year of the Wanli era,
at the Cuizhu Mountain Studio: A Record of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as Seen Through the Elephant-Scratching Parable.
Expounded by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou.
△ Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
whenever reading the commentary, first place the sūtra text upon the desk so that the preceding and succeeding sections may be interconnected; only then can one proceed.
Upon further investigation, this text was composed specifically as a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*; therefore, it is somewhat more detailed regarding that sūtra.

Nevertheless, it merely elucidates points where the general meaning was unclear, where various interpretations differed, or where a particular section, phrase, or character had not yet been explained, rather than providing a complete word-by-word exegesis of the entire work. As for the remaining portions...
This scripture cites only a few sections, and within those sections, only one or two passages are quoted to reveal the general meaning.
It is my hope that those who possess the Way will correct me; it is not that I claim to be right while disparaging others.
Will there be those who find fault with me? I know only how to clarify the Way, and nothing else.
○ Volume One: Translated by Banlamidi;
the terminology translated by Mijia Shijia; the phrasing revised by Xiangshang Fang Rong.
It was transcribed by dictation, and this ancient manuscript contains a reference to the śramaṇa Huaidi of Luofu, who is said to have acted as a "verifier-translator" (zhèngyì);
it is not known why the current edition does not record him. I venture to consider that when a translator first renders Sanskrit into Chinese, the "translator" (yìshě) establishes the meaning;

the "verifier-translator" (zhèngyì) completes the phrasing and sentences; the "scribe" (bǐshòu) polishes the diction and expression; and the "verifier-translator" (zhèngyì) oversees the entire process for the sake of thorough examination and coordination.
This is indeed a matter of collation; for how can the merit of such collation be underestimated? Those who carve the scriptures in the future should include this.

Regarding the division of this scripture into three parts—Preface, Main Text, and Circulation—as established by Wēnlíng and Chángshuǐ, they are largely the same, though within the "Main Text" section...
The division into the five sections—Opening, Seeing, Cultivating, Verifying, and Concluding—is also highly appropriate to the principle.
First, the Section on Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) extends from Ānanda’s request up to the proclamation of the "True Ultimate Nature" within the "Ultimate Meaning";

it causes the practitioner to clearly see for the first time their own eternally abiding true mind as the standard for cultivation. Second, the Section on Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) begins from the second thought-moment of the initial resolve...
The section on the Definitive Meaning explains the divine mantras so that the practitioner may give rise to authentic cultivation based on true insight,
rather than engaging in any separate fabrication apart from the mind. The third section, the Division on Realizing the Path,

ranges from "What is called the Ground of Dry Wisdom" up to "finally exhausting [delusion] to achieve the Wondrous Enlightenment and the Unsurpassed Way," enabling the practitioner to know the true cause and the true fruit.
The fourth section, the "Concluding Summary of the Sutra," explains from what source this sutra is named and instructs that you should uphold it,
so that practitioners may understand how the five types of names and meanings are subsumed within the twenty characters of the current title. The fifth section,

the "Aids to the Path," extends from the hells and the seven destinies up to the most subtle demonic activities, so that practitioners may employ the primary and auxiliary practices in mutual support.
If both the vehicle and the precepts are pursued with urgency, one can swiftly reach the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

Although there may be minor differences in the intermediate sub-sections, these do not pose any significant obstacle; students need only follow the ancient tradition and need not establish new outlines or add superfluous details.
*Mahā-buddhōṣṇīṣa*.
"Great" (*mahā*) refers to the Dharma-Buddha; "Buddha-Usnīsa" (*buddhōṣṇīṣa*) is a metaphor for the Dharma, which is the eternally abiding true mind.
"Usnīsa" means that which is most supreme and unsurpassed among humans. Thus, the Buddha-Usnīsa is the most supreme among the supreme and the unsurpassed among the unsurpassed. As it is said:
When Prince Siddhārtha was held in the arms of those who wished to see the crown of his head, the higher they looked, the higher it seemed; in the end, none could reach it.
This mind extends vertically through the three periods of time, its length and brevity immeasurable; it stretches horizontally across the ten directions, its proximity or distance unfathomable.
To perceive it as free from all marks is likewise so. If one awakens to this mind, then one is a Tathāgata.

The practice-gate of the Bodhisattva stages can be fully expressed in a single phrase. Some claim that this sutra is called "Buddhōṣṇīṣa" because it proclaims mantras from the radiance of the Buddha’s crown;
however, this is merely an incidental indication and not the primary intent. Furthermore, if the three characters are explained individually, they correspond to the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*):
"Buddha" belongs to the Dharmakāya, as True Suchness (*tathatā*) is impartial; "Fo" (Buddha) belongs to Prajñā, as wisdom is perfect.

Because it is fulfilled, the crown [of the head] belongs to liberation; that is, because it is the characteristic of being detached from characteristics, it is also the three greatnesses (trimaṇḍala), divided respectively as essence, characteristic, and function.
One is about to destroy the substance of the precepts.

In my humble opinion, this [incident] was intended by Mātaṅga to destroy Ānanda’s precept-body (*śīla-skandha*). Upon examining the *Supplementary Explanations to the Combined Commentary*, I find that it first accords with my own mind;
this interpretation is most reasonable. Furthermore, it prevents unscrupulous monks from using it as a pretext, which is of great benefit.
Therefore, the text below states: "Because his mind was pure, he had not yet fallen into ruin. If this is so, why would one need supernatural powers?
The mantra was used to protect Ānanda because, although his mind was pure, his power from the Path was still slight, whereas Māra’s intent was firm and his demonic power was intensely blazing.
As they contended for a long time, and he was without rescue or reliance, the matter might have become unpredictable; therefore, protection was necessary.
Since the Sage manifested as an ordinary being, the Dharma should be applied in this manner.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go to protect [the region].

Since the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha’s mantra reaches everywhere without exception, what need was there for Mañjuśrī to carry it? This was merely done in accordance with the formal protocols of the Dharma-gate;
it is like a decree from a Son of Heaven that requires a minister to be dispatched to deliver it to various prefectures and counties. In reality, however—
As soon as the Brahma-voice is raised, its sound pervades the ten directions; it is swift without hurrying and reaches its destination without moving.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom represents the discernment that leads one to abandon Māra and return to the Buddha, turning away from heterodoxy and following the Right Path; this is because wisdom serves as the precursor.
This constitutes the initial expedient for attaining the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* that constitute Bodhi.
"Initial Bodhi" refers to the fruit; the following three refer to the causes; and the "initial expedient" at the end refers to the most urgent and essential practice among those causes.
The general meaning is that one petitions the Buddhas to attain the *śamatha* and *samādhi* that constitute the fruit of the Way.
*Samādhi* is the primary gateway of skillful means (*upāya*) among them. Skillful means belongs specifically to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*), as will be detailed later.
Furthermore, regarding this *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, some have divided the textual passages into sections and made the following correlations:
"from such-and-such a point to such-and-such a point constitutes *śamatha*; from such-and-such a point to such-and-such a point constitutes *samādhi*."

From "a certain place" to "a certain place" constitutes the intent of *dhyāna*: from the inquiry into the mind to the refutation of the two views—the identical and the distinct—it reveals the true through the false;
this is *śamatha*. From "the various illusory floating dusts" to "the eighteen realms," it clarifies the true within the false; this is *samādhi*.
From the question regarding the Middle Way to the conclusion of the section on the "Seven Great Elements," it is both false and true; this is *dhyāna*. Furthermore...
The exposition from the "Investigating the Mind" section through the conclusion of the "Seven Great Elements" belongs entirely to *śamatha*, while *samādhi* and *dhyāna* follow thereafter;
although these differ individually, they essentially analyze the ultimate convergence of the three contemplations and elucidate the great purport of this sutra.
While this is indeed excellent, I fear that beginners, upon hearing this, might become dogmatically attached to such terminology and names.

To claim that the meaning of "wonderful" (miao) refers exclusively to a single section of the sutra is incorrect; rather, the significance of the three contemplations (sanguan) is present throughout the text, which is why it is called "wonderful.

For instance, while the passages concerning the seeking of the mind might seem to pertain to *śamatha*, a careful examination reveals that the inability to find the mind when sought in the seven locations is indeed *śamatha*.
Furthermore, the subsequent discussion regarding the physical body (*rūpakāya*)...
That the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth are all the wondrously luminous true mind is *samādhi*.

That the true mind has no location yet contains the great earth, mountains, and rivers, and that the great earth and mountains have form yet are said to be objects within the wondrous mind is *dhyāna*.
Is it not the case that the three contemplations are fully present? To associate all floating dust-like and illusory transformational phenomena with *samādhi* is indeed subtle.
When contemplating this, the cessation of all marks is *śamatha*; the arising of all marks is *samādhi*;
and their arising in one place and ceasing in another—arising and ceasing simultaneously—is *dhyāna*. Is it not the case that the three contemplations are fully present?
While Ānanda’s request for the definitive meaning of the Middle Way seems to belong to *dhyāna*, upon careful examination, the Buddha said: "Therefore, at this time, I am speaking for you..."

If one asks how the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) can be revealed while further employing worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is clear that what was shown in the preceding passage is none other than the Middle Way.

Furthermore, since it is called *dhyāna*, it must necessarily involve the harmonious integration of emptiness and the provisional, such that the fulfillment of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) goes without saying.
If we rely on the initial passage, where the Tathāgata intends to expound upon *samādhi*...

You say that because your mind has not yet clearly realized the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha*, you cite this to prove the intention of first teaching emptiness and subsequently teaching the provisional (*prajñapti*), thereby judging the initial passage as *śamatha* and the subsequent one as *samādhi*.
You thus categorize emptiness and the provisional as corresponding to *śamatha* and *samādhi* respectively, while treating the middle section as *dhyāna* and so forth;
yet you fail to realize that in the subsequent passages, there are many instances where *samādhi* alone is mentioned.
Following this, it says: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King";
again, it says: "The wondrous path of practice for all samādhis"; again, it says: "Entering samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation";
again, it says: "Attaining samādhi by means of the mark of entering the stream"; again, it says: "If bodhisattvas enter samādhi"; and again, it says: "Desiring..."
"Collecting the mind to enter *samādhi*"; "you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*";
"even if one attains an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*"; "if one speaks great falsehoods, then *samādhi* will not be pure";
"causing their body and mind to enter *samādhi*"; and "all that is true enters *samādhi*."
The *Dì* (地) [Sūtra] further states: "entering samādhi to practice the Dharma-gate"; it also states: "practicing samādhi to seek the Mahāyāna";
it further states: "this pure person practices samādhi"; it also states: "furthermore, there are people who do not rely on true awakening to practice samādhi";
it also states: "you all practice dhyāna to adorn samādhi"; and it also states: "if one attains the wondrous..."
Regarding the term "developing *samādhi*," it is also said that one should dwell in this place and enter *samādhi*;
it is also said that one perfectly illuminates through the clarity of *samādhi*; it is also said that this is the Tathāgata’s true *samādhi*;
and it is also said that within *samādhi*, O sons of good family... Thus, when these instances of *samādhi* are mentioned individually, they all directly take *samādhi* itself as the primary focus.

How can meditative concentration (*samādhi*) be restricted solely to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), such that it must be designated as the "contemplation of the provisional" (*jia guan*) only in contrast to *śamatha*?

There are also one or two instances where *śamatha* is mentioned alone; the same principle applies there. Therefore, one should know that it is unnecessary to forcibly dissect the scriptural texts and rigidly force them into a correspondence with the three contemplations.
I have observed that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks are supremely wonderful and peerless, his physical form translucent like beryl;
I have constantly reflected that these marks are not produced by desire or attachment.
Ānanda, you think that because these wondrous marks do not arise from desire, your resolve to attain them is not incorrect;
yet you do not realize that this very thought is itself the root of the disease. For internally you grasp at your own views and externally you grasp at the marks of the Buddha;

the opposition between subject and object, and the duality of appearance and perception, remain distinct and clear—is this not delusion? Indeed, whether it be the marks of the Tathāgata or the marks of Mātaṅgī, though they are sacred, [they are no different].
Generally, although things appear vastly different, their underlying nature is one and the same.

To cling to the characteristics of illusory, false, and unreal phenomena while remaining ignorant of the mind that is eternally abiding and immutable is to take birth and extinction as the cause while seeking the fruit of non-birth and non-extinction. Thus, the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra says:
"If one perceives the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Cakravartin King would be the Tathāgata. Now...

Why did the Buddha not directly rebuke Ānanda for his error, but instead question him regarding the views and attachments arising from his mind and eyes, thereby gradually shattering his deluded mind and eliminating his deluded views?
This is because while Subhūti understands emptiness, Ānanda clings to signs; thus, the Buddha strikes at the nest to root out the very foundation, forcing his mind to confront [the truth].
When there was nowhere left to place his views and he was pursued to the point of helplessness— where wisdom was exhausted, schemes rendered void,
feelings were at their end, and reason reached its limit— he suddenly attained his own original mind of itself. The subtlety of transformative guidance reaches such a state as this.
There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King.
When Ānanda first sought the mind and directed his thoughts inward, before the Buddha had even finished his response, he immediately spoke these words:
"There is a samādhi... and so forth. Why is this? It is because Ānanda’s original intention was to seek the initial expedient means for attaining samādhi.
The Buddha, perceiving that his mind was directed toward the internal sense bases, specifically challenged him:
"If there were blood beneath the skin, as soon as you first saw the hall, you would have known it must be within the body;
since you did not see it within the body, you know the mind is not within. Since the mind is not within, you know it is also not without, nor is it in between."
Since this applies to all cases, why wait to pursue the investigation section by section until reaching two, three, and even seven?

Therefore, before the answer was finished, he first raised this point to indicate Ānanda’s single point of entry. Once one enters through this point—the initial expedient for *samādhi*—then "one being understood, all are resolved.
Yet, if Ānanda were not a manifestation of great spiritual power (*mahā-upāya*), [he would not have been able to ask such a question].

This analogy illustrates that the profound meaning [of this teaching] is such that the repeated questions and answers, though frequent and tedious, were intended to serve as a model for future generations.

As for the growth of nails, the lengthening of hair, the turning of tendons, and the throbbing of veins—previous commentators have maintained that while one cannot see the internal organs such as the heart and stomach, how could one not know of the nails and veins on the outside? They argue that it is impossible not to perceive them.

I agree that this is correct; however, the two characters "external" (wài) and "floating" (fú) do not accord with the scriptural text. This is because the passage is precisely refuting the notion that the mind resides within;
it would be inappropriate to speak of it as being "external. This is truly because, although nails and hair manifest their entirety on the outside, they actually grow from within;
and although sinews and vessels appear externally, they actually move and vibrate within—therefore, they are all equally internal things.

Specifically, because it has birth, growth, movement, and vibration—qualities that differ slightly from those of the heart and stomach—it is clear that the heart and stomach are indeed difficult to perceive;
yet, since the fingernails and veins can be clearly known, it is evident that the mind cannot reside within them. Thus, it is clear that the mind does not exist inside.
"These bhikṣus have just now come from Śrāvastī, where they went on their alms-round for solid food and returned to the Jeta Grove;
I have already finished my midday meal.
The Buddha has already accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation; why then do you say that the bhikṣus have been begging food from me? The one who understood replied: [as follows].
Regarding the statement that on the day of going to the invitation, Ti-jian (Dīpankara) preached the Dharma for Ānanda and that this should have been separated by a night:
although the sūtra text says that after the meal was finished they returned immediately, Ti-jian and Ānanda reached the Buddha’s dwelling;

and when Ānanda saw the Buddha, he wept and requested the Dharma, with the great assembly simultaneously receiving the holy instructions—this clearly refers to a single assembly on that very day. How can it be said that there was a separation of a night? Now...

This means that since the Buddha possesses a thousand, ten thousand, and a billion transformation bodies—where one body receives offerings in the royal palace and another leads the assembly on almsround—why would this not be permissible?
Therefore, the ancient practice of "pre-emptive fasting" (suozhai) is said to mean preparing for the fast in advance, which is logically unobstructed.

Some say this refers to the ordinary daily routine of begging for food, and this interpretation is also consistent; however, the phrase "just now" (shilai) does not seem to accord with the ordinary routine.
If one sees the eye, the eye would be identical to its object and thus could not function as a follower (*anuvartin*).

If a crystal were placed over the eye, the eye would see the crystal; yet the sense-organ (*indriya*) cannot see the mind that covers it. Even if one were to grant that the eye sees itself, the eye would then become an object (*viṣaya*);
however, it is possible for a sense-organ to see an object, but it is impossible for an object to see an object. As you previously stated, that sense-organ follows [the mind].

If seeing immediately follows from discrimination, then the eye would belong to its object; it could not follow that seeing follows from discrimination, and thus the principle [of the analogy] would fail.
Therefore, it is said that it cannot be established as "following. If one does not see the eye itself, how can one claim that the mind resides within the sense organ?

Furthermore, Wénlíng says that both fact and principle are contradicted: "fact" refers to the metaphor; if the metaphor does not correspond to the phenomenon, it is inconsistent with the facts. This is what is meant.

When facts contradict [the principle], the principle itself is the Dharma; within the Dharma, there is no principle that harbors latent roots. When one does not accord with the principle, it is a contradiction of the principle.
Thus, externally they do not know one another.
Changshui says that the character "not" (不) should be the character "also" (又). This interpretation is highly correct and accords with the supplementary meaning of the treatise;
to claim otherwise, how could one reconcile the meaning of the preceding and following contexts?

If this "not" were indeed present, then the subsequent phrase "body and mind knowing each other" would have to be changed to "body and mind not knowing each other"—is such a principle possible? Thus, he merely clarifies the meaning thereof.
That I did not dare to alter the phrasing reflects the sense of solemnity and care held by the ancients, which applies equally to both Confucianism and Buddhism.
Regarding the two aspects— whether they are taken together or not—

Wenling initially took the sense-objects (*viṣaya*) as the "object" (*vastu*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) as the "essence" (*tattva*), but later he took the sense-objects as the object and the sense-faculties as the essence.

It need not be discussed whether the beginning and end contradict each other as if lacking careful scrutiny. One interpretation holds that both the beginning and the end take the sense-objects (*viṣaya*) as the "thing" (*vastu*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) as the "essence" (*tattva*);
this seems reasonable. However, Tianru states that since the Buddha explicitly spoke of "the essence of this mind," the essence should belong exclusively to the mind.
Another interpretation holds that both the beginning and the end take both the sense-faculties and the sense-objects as the "thing" and the mind as the "essence. Although...

This interpretation is relatively stable and smooth, yet its meaning remains unclear; furthermore, it has been refuted by later scholars on the grounds that the Sūtra itself explicitly states that the eye possesses discernment (*vikalpa*), and that which possesses discernment is not a material object (*rūpa*).
Therefore, I shall now harmonize the aforementioned views with a distinct explanation as follows.
"Possessing both" means being situated between the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*), grasping them simultaneously. "Not possessing both" means being separated from both.

The faculties and objects stand alone in isolation; now you say that both "comprehensiveness" and "non-comprehensiveness" are equally incapable of destroying [the notion that] the mind does not abide in the center.
Why? Because both are untenable. The essence of the mind possesses cognition; it is not devoid of cognition.

Since you have already stated that the eye possesses discrimination while the object of form (rūpa) is devoid of cognition, this means the eye shares the same nature as the essence of the mind in its possession of cognition, whereas only the form...
If it were an insentient object, then the mind would have to stop at merely accompanying the eye; yet you say it "doubles" [its function] by accompanying both eye and form.
How could this not result in a confusion of entities? An entity is not that which possesses knowledge, and the essence of the mind is not the absence of knowledge in an entity.

Since the essence of the mind is precisely characterized by having knowledge as its opposite to insentience, how could it be half-knowing and half-insentient, simultaneously grasping both the sense organ and the sensory object?

Does it abide within them? If you ask how it can be neither both nor not both, you have already stated that while the eye possesses discrimination and the color-object lacks consciousness, consciousness arises between them;
thus, the essence of the mind exists in dependence upon both the sense organ and the object. Now, since it cannot be established as being both, if it does not depend on the organ, it is not knowing;
if it does not depend on the object, it is not non-knowing. That which is neither knowing nor non-knowing is the mind.
Since there is nothing at all, what could possibly be pointed to and called "the characteristic of being within"? Therefore it is said:
"That the mind is in the middle is impossible.
This must be due to not knowing where the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) leads.
The ancient commentary states: "Because of the preceding inquiry, one comes to know that deluded confusion seeks to reach the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Alternatively, it is said: "At this time, Ānanda had not yet recognized delusion; therefore, even speaking of the limit of reality here still pertains to the deluded mind.

This is because, as seen in the following text, he still identifies the capacity for discernment as the mind, and upon first hearing that this is not the mind, he gives rise to alarm and fear. In my humble view, Ānanda has not yet recognized [the nature of his own mind].
To claim that this statement is indeed false, yet to say that the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) is also false, is impossible.
For after the seven investigations, Ānanda’s calculations were exhausted and he sought the Buddha’s instruction regarding the true limit of the mind; what fault could there be in this?

Furthermore, it may be argued that neither the word "false" nor the word "true" appears in the text of the seven investigations; however, why was it not stated at the very beginning that [all things] arise from...?

If one does not realize that the eternally abiding true mind, which is a body of intrinsic purity and luminosity, is being used through various false thoughts, then the two terms "true" and "false" have been manifest for a long time prior to the seven inquiries.

Suppose Ānanda were to say, "I now already know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*)," then the true limit would indeed be false; yet, if he says he does not know, what hindrance is there? If one is too rigidly attached...
If that were so, Ānanda, then your previous question regarding the *śamatha* of bodhi would also have to be false.
As for the statement, "The essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous and can give rise to all conditions;

that which is left behind by conditions," this means that although this *ādāna-vijñāna*—the essence of consciousness—is called "consciousness," this essence of consciousness is in reality the wondrously luminous fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
The substance of this [nature] gives rise to all conditions; there are none that do not originate from it.
It is only because sentient beings follow after delusive conditions that they overlook this primordial luminosity.

Indeed, since beginningless time, sentient beings have spent their entire lives within this fundamental primordial luminosity, yet remain unaware of it, thereby falling into neglect—just as a fish in water fails to recognize the water. This is what is called "forgetting."

The Compassionate One may say that this is not so: how could the luminosity that is inherently present be lost? Yet, one must know that to be deluded regarding what is inherently present is itself called "loss.
It is like the jewel of a strong man; it is not lost, yet it becomes as if lost. This is confirmed by the subsequent scriptural passage where the Buddha says:
"They have lost their true nature and act in a state of inversion."

Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a matter of the shadows of conceptual discrimination regarding mental objects (*dharmas*).
When seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have all been extinguished, then externally one does not follow the flow of sensory distraction, and internally one alone maintains this state.
In this secluded and profound place, do not hastily claim that you have attained your own fundamental mind;
for it remains nothing more than the reflected images of the discrimination of *dharmas*. The fundamental mind is like a mirror, and *dharmas* are like objects;
what is maintained within is merely the reflection appearing in that bright mirror. As the former masters said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Truth, solely because they follow..."
The "pre-conscious spirit" (qian renshi shen) has been the root of birth and death for immeasurable kalpas; deluded people call it the "original person.

When worldly people observe this, they take seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to be the conscious spirit. Once seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have ceased, they assume they have transcended the conscious spirit.
How could they know that, according to this present sutra, these too are merely the nesting place of the conscious spirit and the realm of birth and death?
Although it is the very root, among a thousand or ten hundred people, not even one or two reach this point;
yet even those who do reach it—ten individuals, perhaps five pairs—remain settled in their seats, unable to extricate themselves or let go. Alas!
How many heroes of antiquity and the present have been buried in this obscure place? The secret essentials of Zen contemplation are all revealed herein; let students exert themselves!
Observe Ānanda: your head moves to and fro, yet the seeing remains unmoved; observe my hand opening and closing, yet the seeing remains neither extended nor retracted.
Why is it that you now take movement to be the body and movement to be the object, such that from beginning to end, thought after thought arises and perishes?
You have lost the true nature and act in a state of inverted confusion.
The meaning of the text in this passage is extremely difficult to reconcile. The old commentaries both reject [the views of] ordinary people and those of the Śrāvakas.

It is said that ordinary beings do not know that while the body and its objects are subject to movement, the nature of seeing is unmoving; yet they have no basis for such an argument. However, the body is also unmoving—how can you now claim that movement constitutes the body?
The objects are also unmoving—how can you now claim that movement constitutes the objects? Therefore, it is said: "Regarding the permanent..."
To calculate this as impermanence, although there is some logic to it, it is only at this point that the Tathāgata permits its realization.
The two terms "guest" (āgantuka) and "dust" (rajas) should precisely correspond to taking movement as the body and movement as the environment; thus, both seals [of the teaching] accord with this.

How is it that you suddenly reverse this and condemn it as erroneous? Furthermore, since the preceding and succeeding passages lack any correspondence, it seems like a case of self-contradictory confusion. Now...
Another interpretation follows the literal text with slight elaboration to clarify the Buddha’s intent:
it means that this great assembly regards that which moves as "dust" (*rajas*) and that which does not abide as "guests. Therefore, when observing Ānanda’s head, its movement and shaking are dust;
they are guests, while the seeing itself is without movement. Furthermore, when observing the Tathāgata’s hand opening and closing, [the same principle applies].
Opening and closing are the dust and the guest; seeing them as non-moving is [the true state]. How can it be otherwise?
To clearly know this is to realize that taking movement as the body and taking movement as the environment is a delusion. From beginning to end, thought after thought arises and perishes.

Since one accords with this arising and perishing, one becomes confused about the reality of nature and follows objects with the self. Having lost the reality of nature, one further becomes confused about the emptiness of the environment and clings to objects.
To willingly undergo the cycle of rebirth for one's own sake—is this not truly lamentable? I have provided this interpretation in accordance with the scriptural text;
I do not know whether it is correct or not. [End of] Fascicle Two.

"Hand hanging down" (*chuishou*) refers to being upright, while "hand turned upside down" (*zhengdào*) refers to being inverted. The traditional interpretation holds that holding the hand upright is "inverted" and hanging the hand down is "upright. One theory asserts that hanging the hand down is "inverted," citing the subsequent passage, "Just as when I hang my hand down," as evidence.
Nevertheless, although the scriptural text only mentions, "Just as when I hang my hand down," [the full context remains].
The meaning of these characters generally encompasses the preceding text.
If one says that the passage "As I have hitherto lowered my hand to show the assembly" does not specifically refer only to the lowering of the hand, please clarify this through an analogy:

since the head is considered inverted when it hangs downward, and the hand is likewise considered inverted when it hangs downward, why is it not also considered upright when it is constantly held upward? Furthermore, [the text continues: "And again..."
To say that the hands are not inverted when the head and tail are exchanged at once is based on the false perceptions of worldly people who give rise to notions of inversion;
this subsequent passage serves as the evidence for why they are called "inverted. While this explanation is also excellent, it does not capture the primary intent of the scripture.

This is because the following text describes abandoning the ocean to grasp at bubbles and mistaking the bubbles for the ocean—a complete reversal of the fundamental and the derivative—and thus it is termed "inversion."
The one who knows the ocean represents the True [Mind], while the bubble represents the delusory [body]. The delusory body exists within the mind like a single bubble so minute;

the True Mind pervades beyond the body like the ocean water so vast. To abandon the True and grasp the delusory, to mistake the delusory for the True—this is precisely where the inversion of body and mind resides.
How does this differ from the person who was looking at his hand, whose perception was upright yet whose orientation was mistaken? What is the distinction?
How strange it is that some claim the *He lun* (Treatise on Conjunction) also states that hanging down the hands constitutes inversion. One cannot follow the *He lun* in every respect;

for instance, regarding the "seven investigations" mentioned above, the passage concerning external things not knowing one another, the ancients maintained that the character "bu" (not) should actually be "you" (also), which is a highly correct interpretation.
Although the *He lun* says it should be "bu," the textual meaning ultimately remains不通 (unintelligible) in the subsequent passage.
The argument that "discerning views" and "mutual reinforcement" constitute five layers, and the subsequent critique of this position, is likewise unreasonable.
[The passage] "Obscure darkness constitutes emptiness" (and so forth) leads outward and runs wild.

Changshui [Zhizhou] interprets "obscure darkness constitutes emptiness" through to "binding darkness constitutes form" as corresponding to the three subtle states, and "agglomerating conditions and shaking within" as corresponding to the six coarse states.
The first two "coarsenesses" correspond to the initial stage of rushing outward and running wild; the latter two "coarsenesses" correspond to the final stage of the path of affliction.
Although there are those who object to this correlation, the three "subtleties" are generally explained differently. Now, according to Changshui’s correlation:

the passage on "establishing the objective based on the cause of clarity," the passage on the "aggregates, bases, and elements," and the passage on "the delusive existence of space" are all as follows.

This indicates that the meaning of the preceding and following passages of the sutra text corresponds perfectly, as [the author] attained realization by suddenly awakening from within the state of "pure and fundamental" to the mountains, rivers, and great earth.

Thus, he identified this [state]; furthermore, when孤山 (Gushan) correlates the verse on the nature of Mañjuśrī’s ocean of enlightenment being "tranquil and perfect" with this passage and explains it accordingly, the intent aligns well, clearly showing that 長水 (Changshui) was not without basis for his interpretation.
To say that the preceding and succeeding textual meanings thus correspond to one another and cannot be dismissed is correct.

Furthermore, in my humble opinion, although the "three subtleties" and "six grossnesses" originally derive from the *Awakening of Faith*, when correlating the treatise with the sutra, one need not be overly rigid in matching every phrase and every word;
it is sufficient to grasp the general meaning. This is because the Buddha is the King of Dharma, possessing mastery over all phenomena, and may act according to the occasion.
Expansion and contraction, opening and closing—though the phrasing need not be identical, the underlying principle remains non-dual. To be overly rigid would instead result in contradiction;

how much more so when, within this very treatise, the three subtleties and six coarsenesses together constitute nine aspects, yet upon clarifying the "vital veins" they become eight, and upon tracing the origin of defilement they become six?
Such variations in expansion, contraction, addition, and subtraction are inherently unrestricted within that discourse.
As for those who are led by the Dharma, can they be constrained solely by the laws of death?

To be deluded into taking this as the mind—to be deluded into taking this as the mind—means to clarify that this is not the mind; it is a state of ignorant delusion, mistakenly identifying this which is false and illusory.
If you take this to be your mind, then you must know that you possess a true mind of your own. Why? Because in the preceding passage it was said that "obscuration and darkness become emptiness;
emptiness binds darkness to become form; and form, mixed with thought, becomes the body.

At this time, when there is inner agitation and outward pursuit, a state of murky confusion and turmoil, one identifies this as one's own mind. From this single delusion of taking it for the mind, attachment is born with certainty.
Delusion is taken as the mind within this body, residing in the square inch of the heart, firm and indestructible;
how could one know that this mind is vast and perfect, encompassing empty space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm? Because such inversion exists, they are called those who are to be pitied.
Some say that "this place" constitutes the first delusion regarding the mind, while the passage beginning with "the following place" constitutes the second.
The passage stating, "Delusion is the mind" and further, "it reaches such-and-such a place," is a profound error.
Although this vision is not the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant mind, it is like a second moon.
The second moon is not the true moon. Why does it not return? Although the second moon is not the true moon, there is no second moon apart from the true moon;
this second moon arises directly from the true one, and a person with clear vision certainly sees the true moon straight below.
It is likewise with the seeing-essence: although it is not the true seeing, its entire substance is the true seeing.
If you do not see the place where you do not see, it is naturally not a thing; how could it not be you?
Changshui’s fivefold circular argument and the direct statement of the original intent both ultimately conclude that since seeing is not a thing, how could it not be your true nature?
These two explanations share one meaning; why must they contradict each other?
"If my mind were truly the self, it would cause me now to see that the nature of seeing is the true self;
yet the body is not the self—how does this differ from what the Tathāgata previously refuted, namely, that 'an object can see the self'?
This is a repetition of the preceding text to provide a definitive conclusion. The explanation by Wēn-líng is extremely clear: "Since this [nature of seeing] is already here..."
If the seeing previously described were truly my mind and capable of perceiving objects, then that seeing would be me and this body would not be me.
In that case, the seeing would reside in the object rather than in me; it would be the object coming to see me, rather than me going to see the object.
Is such a principle possible?
"Pointing is not pointing.

One may twist and force together the knotty points [of the text], as this is not the usual practice; therefore, its use is harmless.

For if the original scripture were in Sanskrit and translated into the language of China (Huayan), yet did not employ the characters of this land, it would remain nothing but Sanskrit; how then could it be called a "translation"?

As for those icchantikas who claim that Buddhist scriptures are merely plagiarized from Laozi and Zhuangzi—if that were truly the case, then one would have to translate "Buddha" as "Awakening" (*jue*).
Yi Yin long ago said, "I am one among the people of Heaven who has awakened first.

Since the *Sūtra* was translated using the term "jīng" (經) for what were previously called the *Shī* (詩) and *Shū* (書), the characters "jué" (覺, awakening) and "jīng" (經, scripture) must likewise have been plagiarized from Confucian classics;
thus, such an explanation is untenable and requires no further refutation.
What difference is there between the various non-Buddhist schools who claim that a true self exists pervading the ten directions and this teaching of the Buddha?

This doubt arises because the Buddha speaks of the nature of seeing (*jiansing*) as being pervasive throughout the ten directions, whereas the non-Buddhists likewise speak of a self (*ātman*) pervading the ten directions;

where, then, is the distinction to be found? [The answer] lies in the following passage, which extensively explains the causes and conditions versus spontaneity (*svabhāva*), yet does not resolve this doubt. For indeed, the non-Buddhists...

The calculations of the various paths do not go beyond the two views of annihilationism and eternalism; now, by teaching that both the "causal condition" (*pratyaya-hetu*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) are non-existent, one simultaneously shatters both the view of annihilation and the view of eternity.

Furthermore, by stating that things arise neither from a combination of causes nor from a lack of combination, the realm of emotional attachment is exhausted and the ultimate principle is reached, whereby all conceptual reckonings vanish and the True Self is revealed.
Therefore, it is said: "Perfectly fulfilled Bodhi is the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing; it is the pure original ground."
The mind’s fundamental awakening abiding eternally is what the Buddha refers to as "pervasive";
how could this be compared to the false views of non-Buddhists who cling to the existence of a real self pervading the ten directions?
When one sees the seeing, that seeing is not [the ordinary] seeing; even seeing is already detached from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it.
Regarding the phrase "seeing the seeing," there was an ancient correct interpretation which stated that "being able to see" refers to the seeing that presently perceives objects;
thus, the subsequent character "seeing" (in "seeing the seeing") becomes the "seen. However, "when one sees the seeing" refers to the act of seeing itself, and is not the common seeing of objects.
Therefore it is said: "To see what is not seeing. One interpretation claims that there is no principle by which a true seeing could further see a deluded seeing;

thus, the two instances of the word "seeing" (jiàn) are viewed as level [synonymous], one being true seeing and the other deluded seeing. This interpretation seems plausible but is actually erroneous.

If the two instances of "seeing" are viewed as level, then the two characters "at that time" (shí) would have no place to land. Furthermore, the subsequent text says: "This is truly seeing-seeing; how could there be... [further seeing]?

Regarding the names "Awakening," "Hearing," "Knowing," and "Seeing," how should they be explained and reconciled? Let us test this by applying the analogies found in our own scripture. The Sūtra says:

"If one is to maintain hearing through hearing, why does the Buddha not hear his own hearing? Following this analogy, we say: "If one is to see the Tathāgata through seeing, why does one not see one's own seeing?
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "One does not contemplate the Avalokiteśvara with contemplation. Following this analogy, we say: "One does not see objects with seeing."
When one sees the seer in this manner, the meaning becomes self-evident without needing further analysis.

Regarding "individual karmic delusive vision" (*bipākya-viparyāsa-darśana*) and "common karmic delusive vision" (*sāmānya-viparyāsa-darśana*), the traditional interpretation holds that the former refers to the delusive vision of a single person, while the latter refers to the delusive vision of many people; however, these remain confused and unclear.
It has remained hidden and undeveloped, with no one yet to bring it forth; however, there is a commentary by Wénlǐng which states:

"The 'distinctive karma' (bié yè) refers to the differences in the arising of delusions, while the 'common karma' (tóng fèn) refers to the convergence of the same illusions. Because this was omitted from the *Jìhuì*, lecturers have neglected it.
Wénlǐng merely sketched out its meaning and stopped there, so I shall now explain it in further detail. For example, it is like people in the world who create all manner of things...
Criminals each face different charges; this is likened to being separated. Later, when they encounter the king's law and enter the same prison together, this is likened to being reunited.
What we call "arousing delusion" today refers to creating false karma according to one's mind. Because the causes and conditions for creating karma differ, it is called "distinctive karma.
What we call "experiencing delusion" refers to receiving false retribution according to one's karma. Because the limits of the retribution received are identical, it is called "commonality."
Therefore, they are called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). Furthermore, according to another explanation, while the visual faculty is homogeneous, the objects seen by it may differ;
let the discerning reader examine this in detail according to the traditional interpretation. Thus, the matter is clarified through both its affirmative and negative aspects.
The Sūtra states: "I now clarify these two matters through their progression and regression.

Yet, the old commentaries pass over this section of the text by more than a hundred characters, only reaching the passage concerning "those sentient beings" before declaring it the "progression" (jin) where the same category is applied differently;

and only reaching the passage concerning "a person with impaired vision" before declaring it the "regression" (tui) where the different category is applied similarly. Although the progression and regression are thus made explicit, they are separated from the preceding context by a vast distance, as if—
Wen’eng’s interpretation of the mutual presentation of the dharma and the analogy as a combined clarification through progression and regression seems quite sound;

however, while this achieves clarity, the progression and regression remain somewhat uncoordinated. Jin Suoyin suggests setting aside the shared karma (*sabhāga-karma*) to present a distinct analogy, then applying it to the dharma;

subsequently, setting aside individual karma (*asabhāga-karma*) to present the shared analogy, then applying it to the dharma. What is presented constitutes the progression, while what is set aside [is the regression].
This refers to "retrogression. Combining these two interpretations, their meaning is quite complete.
For example, as it says [in the text]: "Suppose there is a person... This person, for no apparent reason, stares fixedly until his eyes become fatigued.

Regarding this, some say that the character "person" (人) at the top belongs to the Bodhisattva, while the character "person" (人) at the bottom belongs to sentient beings (*sattva*). This is one interpretation.
It is not that the upper and lower [parts] are one and the same person.
One takes a *piṅgala* flask, plugs its two holes, fills it with empty space, and carries it a thousand li away to provide sustenance for another land.
Wenling and Gushan both used the jar as a metaphor for the deluded body and emptiness as a metaphor for the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate).

Jingjue, however, added the phrase "it is like a person," using the person as a metaphor for karma; this is correct according to the *He lun* (Compendium). Furthermore, the *He lun* states that emptiness is a metaphor for consciousness:
non-discrimination is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while discrimination is the *vijñāna-skandha*. This is because the space within a jar is limited.

There is a distinction between conceptual differentiation and external emptiness. Wēnnéng claims that one should block both holes [of the vessel], yet he does not understand what constitutes "sameness" and "difference.
Now, I say that blocking the holes is intended to prevent objects from escaping outside the jar;
since the jar has two holes, blocking both is the ultimate measure of protection. Emptiness is not something that enters or exits, and yet—
The metaphor of "carefully blocking" refers to recognizing that the fundamental root is illusory while maintaining that illusory life-force, fearing only its loss;
the metaphor of "using provisions for a thousand li" refers to wandering through many kalpas, dying here and being born there.
○ Third: [The argument] that the visual faculty must first perceive external objects before they can be seen refutes the view that seeing does not arise from space.
If seeing were to arise from space, then space would necessarily first perceive external objects before [seeing occurs].
It is said that space is the "seer" (*darśana*) and material forms are the "seen" (*dṛśya*).
Now, if this eye-faculty truly resides within my face, then I myself would be a material form. Space ought, conversely, to turn back and see my own eye-faculty.
If it cannot see the eye, then the principle of its gazing outward at external forms is not established. How, then, could seeing arise from space?
"Seeing and hearing flow against the current, a state where the current cannot reach.

According to the interpretation of Master Gushan, this "flowing against the current" of seeing and hearing is as follows: while the five sense-faculties follow the current, it is only the mind that can turn back;
thus, its seeing and hearing flow against the current to take the five objects as conditions. Because it flows against the current, it grasps these objects to form recollection. This is the flow.
Regarding that which does not reach the ground: such a limit of the counter-flow, being beyond reach, is then utterly silent and oblivious, having no object of perception;
because the flow does not reach it, memory is lost and one becomes forgetful.
It is said that "sound comes to the side of the ear.
However, the *Śruti* (Scripture) clearly states that it is not the case that sound comes to the side of the ear. Now, if we examine this through empirical evidence, there are points of doubt.
For example, suppose a bell tower or drum tower stands at the very center between the north and south sides of a city; if a south wind arises, then [the sound from the north would be obstructed].
When the southern city hears it, the northern city does not; when the wind arises, the southern city hears it, yet the northern city does not.
How is it that the sound is conveyed by the wind so that people can hear it? How could one say that the sound does not come to the ear?
Most people have carelessly overlooked this point without raising an objection. In my humble opinion, how could the Buddha’s words possibly be in error? Sound certainly does not come to the ear.

The meditative concentration of the peripheral mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm; yet, because sentient beings become attached to stillness and give rise to listening, they lose their original wondrous perfection, which becomes localized and obstructed, bound and made small.
Thus, when the wind is favorable, one hears it, but when the wind is adverse, one does not.
This is the fault of the ear for being driven by external conditions and lacking self-mastery; it is not the fault of the sound. By inferring from this, [one understands that] even when separated...
When a wall transmits sounds, they can be heard both near and far; this, moreover, presents a difficulty.

Since the wall does not obstruct sound, why is it that when one person inside the city speaks facing the wall and another person outside the city listens against the wall, there is suddenly nothing to be heard?
This is also the same as the previous case: it is a fault of the ear, not due to the wall or the city. Therefore—

As for the supernormal power of the ear, it is the faculty of penetrating hearing; one may hear a single world-system, or even as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, without exhaustion.
As for this which is known through touch, who is it that can touch?
Generally, for all things, it requires that one possesses the capacity [to act] and the other possesses the capacity [to receive], such that they mutually interact before contact can be established;
thus, one must have cognition while the other lacks it. Now, when one rubs the head with the hand, both the hand and the head each possess cognition.

With which of these should one designate the "agent of contact"? If the hand were the agent of contact, then the head would be like wood or stone. Since the head also possesses cognition, how can it be so designated?
If the head were the "toucher" and the hand were merely wood or stone, then since the hand also possesses cognition, how could it be called "touch"?

This clarifies that the body's perception of touch is entirely illusory. Question: If the hand rubbing the head does not constitute "touch," then when the hand rubs an external object, would that not constitute "touch"?
Answer: This, too, is a false distinction between subject and object. However, this is the common understanding of people.
Because it is difficult to clarify, we borrow the example of the head and hands to introduce the point that the body is ultimately empty and false, just like the head and hands.
From the perspective of transformation, the characteristics of the transformed realms are themselves non-existent; from the perspective of non-transformation, they are eternal.
Since [the sense of touch] arises from form, it should not be able to cognize the location of empty space.
The preceding passage stated that if this consciousness arises from form, then when form ceases, the consciousness should likewise cease;

since both would have ceased together, emptiness alone would remain, and who then would cognize that emptiness? If, at the time form ceases, the consciousness does not cease along with it, then the consciousness alone would remain without form as its companion, and who would experience that emptiness?
Now, once again reiterating the previous point, it is said that not only would the consciousness remain without a realm [of objects].
If consciousness were to undergo transformation and cessation in accordance with form, then consciousness itself would have already ceased; who then would constitute the element of space?

It is not merely that consciousness ceases—it should not even be possible for consciousness to perceive space. Conversely, if consciousness does not undergo transformation and cessation, it would eternally be of one substance with form and have no connection to space;
who then would perceive space? Through such repeated examination, it is clear that visual consciousness does not arise from form.
If they unite, there is a center; if they separate, there are two.
This follows from the preceding argument that visual consciousness does not arise from the eye nor from form.
Since it does not arise separately from these two locations, must it not arise by uniting both locations? Yet, when you wish to unite them, they are separated in the middle.
For the eye belongs to that which possesses cognition, while form belongs to that which lacks cognition;
since that which possesses cognition and that which lacks cognition stand in opposition to one another, how could they possibly be united? If you wish to separate them, they are already united.

This is because the faculty of the eye must necessarily unite with form, and the object of form must necessarily unite with the eye, before consciousness arises between them; thus, the two aspects meet and harmonize. How could this be?
How can they be separated? If joined, they separate; if separated, they join. Since this essential nature is thus chaotic and indistinct, where could one establish a boundary for their co-arising?
Having previously clarified that the eye and forms are illusory, and now stating that consciousness is also illusory, it is said that all three locations are non-existent.
Furthermore, regarding your consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) and its nature of both deliberation and discernment—do they constitute the same or are they different?

According to the traditional interpretation, the first phrase refers to the mind (*manas*), while the subsequent two phrases refer to consciousness (*vijñāna*). However, since the first phrase explicitly designates it as "consciousness-mind," how can it be taken as the mind?
I maintain that the first phrase should still be understood as consciousness, while the following two phrases refer to the mind; for it is the mind to which [the functions of] deliberation belong.

"Discernment (*manasikāra*) is also capable of cognizing. This means: is the meaning of this consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) and that of the discernment of the mind (*manas*) the same or different?
If consciousness were identical to the mind, then consciousness would be the mind itself; how then could it be said to be produced by the mind?
If consciousness were different from the mind, then consciousness would be devoid of cognition and separated from the mind; how then could it be said to be [the mind]?"

As for that which gives rise [to consciousness]: if consciousness were distinct from the mind (*manas*) and yet capable of deliberation and discernment, then the mind would be without cognition while consciousness possesses cognition;
one would have to reverse consciousness back into the mind to constitute consciousness. Furthermore, how could it be said that what arises from the mind is identical [to it] and cannot be different?
Since consciousness does not arise from the mind, why should there be any doubt? How then can one claim that [consciousness] is based upon the mind?

Regarding the "elements" (*dhātu*), it is not that there is only one. One school of thought asserts that both the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) and the deliberating intention (*manas*) are capable of discernment;
since both are capable of discernment, they are identical. How can you then ask whether they are the same or different?

Since both are capable of discernment, they possess consciousness (*vijñāna*). How can you then ask whether there is consciousness or no consciousness? Some claim that the mental intention (*manas*) and the deliberating consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perform discernment; this is what is being discussed now.

Why is it that *manas* (the mind) also includes the function of discernment (*vijñapti*)? It is because the three—*citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*—have been traditionally said to be interchangeable in meaning.
As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states, "The faculty of *manas* discriminates all phenomena. Thus, why should *manas* not also include discernment? There is nothing improper about it.

He clearly realized for himself that he had attained his original, wondrous mind, which is eternally abiding and indestructible. (This section should follow the passage "If empty, it is the same as nothingness.

As above, through this subtle and profound instruction, he resolved his own mind and vision, leading up to the revelation that the five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, the six consciousnesses, and the seven elements are all the Tathāgata-garbha mind;
because of this realization, he understood that his own mind is eternally abiding and indestructible.
To extinguish this is the great purport and the great eye of this sutra. If one truly attains this mind, then I shall always be the host and all phenomena shall be guests;
though Chang'an may be bustling, my kingdom remains tranquil.
That Mātanga woman is like a malevolent fox that, upon suddenly encountering a bright mirror, has nowhere to hide or crouch—what power could she possibly exert her sorcery?
"Since you adjusted your robes, why do you sweep [them] upside down?
Because of these four characters, "Since you adjusted your robes," there have been various interpretations; now, following the text as it stands, its meaning will become clear:
this is to clarify that the wind does not arise from that side. If one were to say that the wind arises from that side...
If the wind were to come from that face to here and brush against you, Ānanda, then this wind—manifesting as it brushes that face while you adjust your robe—would have arisen at that face;
why then does it not blow favorably toward you, but instead blows in reverse against that face?
Therefore, one knows for certain that the wind does not arise from that face. If you attribute this reverse blowing to Ānanda, then it is not a clear wind.
The wind arises from that face; it does not arise from Ānanda’s *kāṣāya*.
The perception of seeing is devoid of cognition, existing only because of form and space.

Some may say that while this passage states the perception of seeing is devoid of cognition, the subsequent text contrasts the emptiness of the perception of seeing with its stubbornness; thus, [it follows that] the perception is...
There are those who understand the contradiction between "upper" and "lower" by assigning the upper "awakening" (*jue*) to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the lower "awakening" to cognition;
while this seems reasonable, one should not interpret a single term in two ways. Now, when it is said that there is no cognition, it does not mean there is truly no cognition.
This is intended to introduce the phrase "in relation to form and emptiness," for when form and emptiness do not appear, the seeing-awakening is quiescent.
Yet it is as if there were no knowing; it is only after the manifestation of emptiness through form that one perceives the awakening of knowing.
Confucius said, "What do I know? I know nothing. When someone asks me a question, I strike at both ends and exhaust the matter.
Confucius was truly without knowledge; who else could answer questions? To compare two states of non-knowing—this is an extremely profound and exhilarating insight.
When the nature perceives through the clarity of awareness, and awareness perceives through the clarity of the spirit, one understands the seven elements as being of a single pattern.
The first element, "Greatness," states: "The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form.

This means that truth and delusion are fundamentally of the same nature: form that is entirely of this nature is itself emptiness, and emptiness that is entirely of this nature is itself form. It is just like...
To say that the entirely moist wave is water, and the entirely moist water is the wave;

To say that the sight which is entirely nature is clarity, and the clarity which is entirely nature is sight; and so on, up to the "Great [Element] of Consciousness," saying "the nature of consciousness..."

The "awakening to clarity" (*jue-ming*) refers to true consciousness (*zhen-shi*), which is also called the consciousness that is entirely of the nature (*quan-xing*). To know this is to know the knowledge that is entirely of the nature; thus, knowledge is itself consciousness.

This is the same principle as the mutual interpenetration of the True and the Conventional in the *Seven Greats*. Regarding the latter two "Greats" [space and consciousness], Wēn-líng’s interpretation differs from the previous five.

Furthermore, when the four great elements such as earth are said to "use" the character for space (*kong*), it refers to their coarse and subtle aspects; the Great Space uses awakening (*jue*) as its function.

The term "character" (*zi*) refers to that which is both insentient and sentient. To see the great function is called "seeing" (*jian*); seeing is deluded seeing, whereas "clear seeing" (*ming jian*) is true seeing.
To cognize the great function is called "cognition" (*shi*); cognition is deluded cognition, whereas "true cognition" (*zhen zhi*) is true knowing.
If it were empty space, it would be identical to nothingness and not a distinct entity; even if you were to activate your consciousness therein, what could you possibly discern?
This clarifies that consciousness certainly does not arise from empty space. If it were to arise from empty space, it would be neither a characteristic (*nimitta*) nor a seeing (*darśana*).

This passage has three turns of meaning: the great sounds of the world are easily heard by people, yet the sound of a mosquito is the most subtle of all sounds.
First, an extremely subtle sound may still be heard when listening from nearby; yet now it is at a distance of a hundred paces.
Second, even those with keen hearing find it difficult to hear the sound of mosquitoes and gnats from afar; yet now it is further compounded by the fact that the listener is deaf.
If this is so, then since the form of the mosquito cannot even be seen, how could its sound possibly be heard? This is the analogy for the Dharma.
First, the subtle and wondrous principle of the ultimate truth is profound and abstruse, like the sound of a mosquito;

The meaning of this passage is self-evident. Some claim that the body of a mosquito represents the *satyadharma* (Ultimate Truth) and the sound of a mosquito represents the *paramārtha-satya* (First Principle of the Middle Way).

Yet, because it has never failed to be quiescent, it is called "wondrously luminous" (*miaomiao*). The hundred physical constituents are governed by the mind; there is an interpretation that these six characters lie at the very center of this mantra and thus call it the "Mantra of the Mind.
However, when examined in light of the preceding and following texts, it is clear that they do not occupy the central position, and the error [of such an interpretation] is evident.
Based on this adherence and relying upon this, the emphasis in the ten subsequent sections lies in the words of the mantra; the mantra possesses vast and wondrous powers.
By virtue of this, there is not a single Tathāgata throughout the ten directions who has not relied upon it, upheld this vehicle, and transmitted it to achieve various wondrous functions.
This being so for even the Buddhas, how much more so for ordinary beings? Now, I shall briefly provide ten metaphors for those who rely on this mantra-heart.
This mantra is the mother of all Buddhas; it is the true seed that gives birth to the Tathāgatas. Therefore, the Buddha must...

It is the sovereign seal of the Buddha; therefore, the Buddha must always uphold it when receiving a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). Those who rely upon this mantra-heart receive their prophecy based on it.
This mantra is the abode of the merit of peace and security; it is the supreme banner that transcends all fear.
Therefore, the Buddha must rely upon it to rescue others from suffering and deliver them from calamity. Those who follow this mantra-heart accord with awakening.

This essence is the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels that fulfills all desires from the mind; therefore, the Buddha necessarily follows it to universally make offerings to the sages and worthies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
For those who practice this mantra-heart, this mantra is unimpeded and penetrating; it is the great thoroughfare shared by thousands of sages and ten thousand worthies.
Therefore, the Buddha necessarily practices it to gather in the proximate causes and open the secret treasury.
For those who recite this mantra-heart, this mantra is ultimately complete and perfect; it is the solemn decree of the Dharma King issued to the myriad nations.
Therefore, the Buddha certainly recited it to achieve Perfect Enlightenment and enter Nirvana.

To transmit this mantra-heart is to ensure that this mantra endures forever without extinction; it is the inexhaustible great lamp of wisdom that universally illumines both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Therefore, the Buddha necessarily transmitted them so as to leave behind his transformation for ten thousand generations.

the Buddha originally taught people to maintain the *dhāraṇī*, yet now all of it has been categorized as separate methods, while the *dhāraṇī* originally maintained is [neglected].
On the contrary, it results in uselessness by taking the guest as the host; this is the first error. Mantras are the essence of Esoteric Buddhism, yet now they have become Exoteric teachings;

Furthermore, there are two characters that are identical; yet, to take this as the "Three Prajñās" and to take this as the "Three Bodhis" is utterly devoid of meaning—this is the fifth error.

it is inappropriate to arbitrarily establish ten categories. For mantras are fundamentally a single thing—the merit of recitation—and while there may be ten [instances of recitation], the mantra itself has never been ten.
Its eighth error is that, having already stated there are "ten sets of three dharmas," their Sanskrit terms ought to be distinct one by one;

Its ninth error is that, if you claim the sutra contains seven fruits of permanence, the script of the sutra merely mentions "seven fruits"—how can you forcibly expand them into ten, such that each fruit becomes a single, undifferentiated whole?

Returning to oneself is entirely encompassed, without exception, within these four characters of the "Perfect and Sudden" (*yuantun*) Dharma-gate. As Master Gushan said:

This is the emergence of the semblance of the true; from the provisional name to the ultimate truth, it is unified by a single principle—how wondrous these words!
The "name" refers to the stage of abiding in faith.

Wuxing’s critique is correct; however, one need not be so rigidly attached to this word "abiding" (zhù). This is because the text of this sutra is composed of four-character phrases;

thus, while the "mind of faith," "mind of mindfulness," "mind of wisdom," and "mind of concentration" all contain the word "abiding," the "mind of diligence," "mind of non-retrogression," "mind of attaining the Dharma," and "mind of dedication" in between lack this word.
This pattern continues until the ninth "mind of precepts" and the tenth "mind of vows."

Otherwise, since the initial "zhù" (住) is already established as a distinct division, every subsequent sentence ought to contain the character "zhù. Why, then, would it sometimes be present and sometimes absent?

The fact that the various stages prior to the bhūmis are collectively treated as a single stage, the ten bhūmis plus the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) constitute eleven dwellings,
and the Tathāgata constitutes one dwelling— making thirteen dwellings in total— and the uniform application of the term "dwelling" (vihāra) to each, is sufficient evidence [for this].
This awakening marks the initial attainment of the Vajra-mind, the first stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*).
It is not necessary to laboriously investigate whether this is identical to or different from the preceding Dry Wisdom; for it is both identical and different, and different and identical.
However, if one proceeds through the text according to its sequence, the meaning will become manifest of itself. Now, I shall explain each word in turn: "this awakening" refers to...
"Attaining Equal Enlightenment for the first time" means that while the preceding stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-prajñā) merely revealed its initial signs, its full substance had not yet been attained;
now, for the first time, it is attained. "Vajra-mind" refers to the wisdom within the Mahāyāna mind.

"Dry Wisdom" indicates that one has not yet interfaced with the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment. As for why Dry Wisdom is necessarily called "initial": [it is because it marks the beginning of the path].

This clearly explains that the primordial wisdom at the very beginning, having passed through the stages of faith, abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds, is only now attained in its entirety.
Because the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition and the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause, they are different yet identical;
because the cause is not the fruition and the fruition is not the cause, they are identical yet different.
