the various explanations are not uniform. Wēn-líng [Lín-lèi] takes "faith in the Dharma" (*dharmābhiśraddhā*) through "the equality of gold" (*tulyasuvarṇa*) as the twelve heavens, but this is said to be inconsistent with the principle, as it treats "gold" both as the traverser and the traversed.
Wú-xīng [Zǔōng-jì] takes "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "abiding" (*sthiti*)...

However, this combination is not particularly secure, nor is the meaning of "single" and "double" entirely satisfactory.

Each stage consists of ten, forming a composite set of twelve; this is followed by the single stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana*). This is then followed by the composite stages of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Direction;

after these composites, they are followed by the single stages of the four practices of application (*prayoga*); after these singles, they are followed by the composite stages of the ten grounds (*bhūmi*);
after these composites, they are followed by the single stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*), and so on up to Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Thus it is.
It is said that the layers of explanation are most subtle and wondrous.
Regarding these fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi, there are many interpretations;
however, only Wu-xing maintains that the preceding stage of "Dry Wisdom" (gan-hui) is excluded from the enumeration, as it arises solely through...

"The Sūtra speaks of the 'true path to Bodhi,' which reveals that Dry Wisdom is not the true state of wondrous enlightenment, nor is it a path. This explanation is most appropriate.

One alternative explanation takes the character "jian" (see) above as "xian" (manifest), thus reading it as "manifestly seeing a single faculty. This meaning is also plausible;
however, neither the character "xian" nor "jian" carries the intended sense here.

Combining with the category of the gentle, some may doubt that resentment serves as the cause; having completed their time in hell, they become malevolent ghosts and poisonous creatures, and upon reaching the human realm, they become wolves—thus cause and effect are similar.
As for those whose cause was arrogance, having emerged from hell, they transmigrate through successive states until...

Humans belong to the category of the yielding, whereas arrogance is its opposite; yet why is it that those who belong to the yielding category [sometimes] become so? This is because there are various kinds of retributions:

there is the retribution of past habits (*pūrvābhyāsa-vipāka*) and the retribution of opposites (*pratidvandva-vipāka*). Thus, the fierce and violent may be transformed into tigers and wolves, while the greedy may be transformed into sheep and dogs;
this is called the retribution of past habits. Those who are excessively extravagant may be transformed into poverty, and the deceitful and fraudulent... [into ignorance].
That a person transforms into one who is foolish and ignorant is called a retributive response of opposition; what belongs here is the case of opposition.
For one who was haughty in the past and looked down upon others now becomes one who is looked down upon by others. This "yielding" (róu) does not refer to being gentle, mild, or compliant;
rather, it refers to being timid, weak, and listless—qualities by which everyone treats one with ease.
Regarding "firmly adhering to the practice of ingesting" (and so forth): "firm adherence" refers to both the ingestion of plants and the plants themselves;

while these two matters appear similar, they differ. The practice of ingestion is called the *āhāra-mārga* (the path of food), referring to such things as sesame, lotus seeds, and water chestnuts, as these are what are commonly consumed.
The plants themselves are called the *bhaiṣajya-mārga* (the path of medicine), referring to such things as yellow-root (*huángjīng*), pine, and cypress, which are medicinal substances.
Because it is commonly used, the Way of Food can merely prolong one's years; the Way of Medicine, however, can enable one to ascend lightly.
Wēnlíng should not substitute the ingestion of medicinal herbs for the consumption of food; the latter is a matter belonging to the second category [of practice].
The "firm union" (*khaṇḍakhaṇḍa*) is continuous and without cessation.
The ten types of *siddhas* begin with the ingestion of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and culminate in transformation (*vikriyā*); indeed, each subsequent stage is more profound than the preceding one.
Regarding the ninth [stage], "union," it cannot be explained according to ancient interpretations that take the internal *kaṇṭha* and *li* as corresponding to external male and female.

Sexual union is purely an internal matter; what that book refers to as "taking from the *kan* to fill the *li*," "extracting lead and adding mercury," and even "dragon, tiger, crow, hare, infant, maiden, and Huangpo" are all metaphors.

Since it does not even permit one to identify the heart and kidneys with the *li* and *kan*, how much less could it allow for the sexual arts of men and women, which are the lowest of the low? As Qing'an said, these are merely "lustful men and women."
Those who crave profit engage in this; it is the way of great chaos. How could one ever cease [from such pursuits]?
At the ninth stage, one transcends prior thoughts and contemplates subsequent transformations, yet instead produces base, vulgar, and obscene perverse accomplishments. The Sūtra says:

"These individuals also refine their minds among human beings, but because they do not cultivate the Samādhi of Right Enlightenment, they do not depart from delusive thoughts and do not emerge [from saṃsāra]."
Even those in the cycle of saṃsāra may encounter a single point of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma that transforms them, whereby they will surely attain awakening,
as was the case with the Realized Man Lü Yán regarding Huánglóng.
He lived for ten million years.
Among the vows of the Great Master of Nanyue, one states: "May I become an immortal of long life and behold Maitreya";
another states: "May I attain longevity and strive to seek the Buddha-way"; and the third states: "For the sake of seeking the Mahāyāna, I vow to enter the deep mountains."
The Great Sage quickly achieved accomplishment; as for the holy sages who manifested at Mount Nanyue, what was it they sought?

It was precisely because that which is not taken up by the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* arose from their original vows: to behold Maitreya, to seek the Buddha-way, and to study the Mahāyāna—not for the sake of longevity.
Furthermore, it is said that they did not cherish their own bodies or lives when they made these vows. How could worldly people treasure such illusions?
One might hope that this body could attain longevity; however, within these traditions there are further claims regarding external elixirs (*waidan*) and internal elixirs (*neidan*).
When foolish people encounter such things, they may give rise to false views. Beginners should simply maintain firm faith in the present scripture as the Buddha’s word;
as for what was said by [Hui]neng of Mount Nanyue, it may be set aside for now.

"Not allowing the mind to flow errantly toward sexual misconduct" does not mean merely failing to engage in it while remaining free from such flow; rather, it means being able to restrain the mind within the context of sexual misconduct so as not to commit it.
One must not misinterpret this scriptural passage, as doing so would foster wrong views.
"Ascending to the Subtle and Refine" (and so forth): the three calamities do not reach it.
Regarding Tuṣita, among the four heavens of the Desire Realm, it is called "Ascending to the Subtle and Refine," "Not Reaching the Lower Realms," and "The Three Calamities Do Not Reach It.

Commentators claim that all these names refer to the Inner Court; this seems plausible. However, since there is no ultimate end to that heaven, it would be illogical for it not to be mentioned [in this context].
Now, if one tastes this carefully, it is clear that the meaning lies beyond the words; that the "original celestial station" need not be discussed further is self-evident.

As for those who transcend all categories, ascend to the subtle and refined, and even reach the point where they are not affected by the three calamities—though they are called the Inner Court, in general they are all designated as Tuṣita Heaven.
In the ninth fascicle,
it adds "clarity and awakening.
Although the sutra speaks of "purity of the precepts" and adds "clarity and awakening," this so-called "clarity and awakening" does not refer to the awakening of the mind that realizes the Way.
This means that one has merely awakened to the fact that desire is not worth coveting or cherishing;

however, as stated in the subsequent passage—"If one awakens to wisdom through a mind of equanimity, one becomes an Arhat and enters the Bodhisattva vehicle"—this "awakening" is what constitutes true enlightenment.
The Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (and so forth) is called the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
Why is it that "immeasurable" is now divided into the preceding and succeeding [stages] of shallow and deep?

It is because the previous mention of physical and mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) implies that both the external physical form and the internal thoughts are purified; thus, it is said to be "immeasurable," which extends throughout the entire body.

When the mind is immeasurable, yet the body and mind remain unpurified externally, it is not yet called "Universal Purity. As stated later, when the world, the body, and the mind—the primary retribution of the body and mind—are purified, and the world, the environment—the secondary retribution upon which they depend—are also purified, only then is it named Universal Purity (*Parishuddha*).
Among these, only the *ālaya-vijñāna* remains in its entirety, while the *manas* is only half-subtle.
The *He lun* (Compendium of the Meaning) and Changshui’s commentary state that the "half-subtle" aspect belongs to the six consciousnesses;
however, the two preceding lines connect with this [point] somewhat difficult to reconcile. The masters of Wenglun all attribute the "half-subtle" aspect to the *manas*, and Wenglun judges it thus.

If there were no longer six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*) in that state, then the subsequent passage stating that "the mind of consciousness is entirely extinguished" would have to be understood as referring to the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*); otherwise, since the six consciousnesses are already absent, what consciousness would be extinguished?

Previously, I relied on the commentary by Wēnlíng, who maintained that "the mind of consciousness is entirely extinguished" yet the nature of consciousness (*vijñānatā*) has not perished, and thus it was unimpededly understood as referring to the eight consciousnesses.
Now, reflecting further, I consider that this is ultimately not quite satisfactory; therefore, I shall adopt the meaning of the previous treatise and commentary to revise this.

To clarify this teaching, it is said that herein the coarse portions of the six consciousnesses have already ceased, leaving only the fundamental Ālaya-vijñāna in its entirety, while Manas and the six consciousnesses do not take form or space as objects, but only their subtle half-portion by internally cognizing them;
thus, it is only when the lower levels of consciousness and mind are entirely extinguished that this half-portion is finally extinguished. Nevertheless, although this half-portion is subtle...
It would be better if the four characters "must obtain" (須得) were added before "those six consciousnesses" (與彼六識); perhaps there is a textual omission?

One interpretation holds that the flow of the six consciousnesses has not yet been entirely extinguished; furthermore, while it is said they are "extinguished" based on their general state, this is an appearance of extinction that is not actually extinction.
That celestial king is a bodhisattva dwelling in *samādhi*. It is not that all such celestial kings are definitively bodhisattvas;
as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*bhūmi*) mostly become kings of Jambudvīpa;
those of the second stage become wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*); and so on up to the celestial kings of the six desire realms and the Great Brahmā King."
The phrase "for the most part" (*duōdē zhī yīzì*) means that for the majority it is so; however, there are also times when this is not the case.

When a single person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, "truth" (*zhēn*) is spoken in contrast to delusion (*wàng*), and the "source" (*yuán*) is spoken in contrast to the derivative (*mò*). Although truth is inherently possessed, it remains hidden and fails to manifest as one pursues delusion and flows away from the source.
Delusion prevented its return to the source; now, by giving rise to the true mind, it returns once more to its original foundation.
In the realm of the true source, not even a speck of dust can stand; how could empty space fail to dissolve away?
"All these spaces of the ten directions are now utterly extinguished.

As for the previous statement that one shall never hear of space being decomposed or destroyed, and the present claim that space is extinguished—why do these preceding and following words seem contradictory?
There are two meanings to this: first, the gate of contrasting the empty and the real; in the world, real phenomena exist...
That which arises must necessarily perish; empty space has no form and neither arises nor perishes, for it has never been heard to decay or disintegrate.
Second is the gate of the contrast between the real and the delusive: when all things are contrasted with empty space, all things are delusive;
when empty space is contrasted with True Suchness (*tathatā*), empty space is also delusive. Delusive confusion gives rise to empty space, yet when returning to the Real, there is no empty space.

Therefore, even empty space can be extinguished and dissolved. Thus we know that empty space is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent; its existence and dissolution depend upon one's own mind.

For those whose minds are deluded and who perceive objects as external, empty space appears distinct and pervasive. For those who realize that objects are nothing but the mind, where is there any empty space?
Consequently, when the empty space of one person is extinguished and dissolved, the empty space of many people is not thereby extinguished; these two states do not obstruct one another.

Furthermore, although Chang’an is bustling, my country is tranquil; thus, while the land of one person is tranquil, the Chang’an of many people is naturally bustling—these two states are mutually unimpeded.
They see their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason, and the great earth tremble and split; whether aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial, all are struck with terror.
Ordinary people, shrouded in darkness, do not perceive these transformations.
When a practitioner enters the state of dhyāna, the various māras naturally witness their palaces collapsing and the great earth shaking and splitting.
Originally, when the land surged upward, the multitudes were struck with terror and awe; yet ordinary people, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive the transformation.
That this state was seen only by the demons while humans remained unaware was surely due to their own obscurity. Although humans are obscured, they are more spiritual than other things;
since each thing was startled by the event, why do humans fail to perceive it? Is it that humans are actually inferior to these things? Now...
This means that those who do not awaken are not entirely unconscious like wood or stone; they simply fail to perceive the transformations brought about by the power of the practitioner’s samādhi.
Furthermore, when such worldly events as mountain collapses and earthquakes occur, people experience fear just as objects do.

Moreover, "transformation" (yì) refers to movement and shifting, while "mutation" (niè) refers to strange anomalies; it is during the time of samādhi that both ordinary beings and sages undergo these changes.
This autumn is the season when the orthodox and the heterodox wage war; therefore, there is restless agitation and unpredictable anomalies.
Take for example Mātaṅgī, who was exceedingly lowly and inferior; she merely used a mantra to destroy your observance of the Buddha’s Vinaya, ruining but one precept among the eighty thousand.
Because your mind was pure, you have not yet fallen into ruin. This [present situation], however, will destroy your...
The "Treasure-Awakening Whole Body" refers to the Vinaya, which is the precepts—one of the eighty thousand practices. This phrase corresponds to the following passage:
Mātangī is weak and inferior, while the various māras are fierce and powerful; she counters them by destroying the single precept against lust, thereby restoring your treasure.
To realize that one’s entire body has not yet exhausted the outflows (*āsrava*) is a minor fruit compared to the great resolve of truly returning to the source;
to lose one's fundamental nature for the sake of such a minor fruit is like the ruin of a commoner's household, which is hardly worth mentioning.
Yet, to lose the success of the great resolve is like the confiscation of the estates of a noble lineage—this is truly lamentable.
In this context, one should investigate the wondrous clarity with precision.

Within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), such expressions as "investigating the wondrous clarity," "investigating internally and externally," "ultimate transparency," "profound investigation," and "the pinnacle of refined investigation" directly reveal the essential and true core of Chan practice.
In one's practice, one must not weary of repetition; this is where the student should concentrate their spirit, exhaust their thoughts, and exert their utmost brilliance.

If the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, although the other four aggregates remain clearly present—within the Buddha’s Bodhi being neither fully realized nor yet fully realized—the momentum for breaking through the bamboo has already been established and the mechanism for overturning the precipice can no longer be resisted.
There is a path to enter by cutting the pass and seizing the gate; it is simply...

I fear that one might settle for little and become complacent, thereby limiting oneself and failing to advance; yet, to shatter this aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is no small matter—it cannot be accomplished merely by speaking of it.
A practitioner must exert effort and engage in a decisive battle before success can finally be attained.
At that time, the *hun*, *po*, *yi*, *zhi*, and *shen*—with the exception of that which clings to and receives the body—all interpenetrate and act as host and guest to one another.
Medical treatises maintain that the *hun* belongs to the liver, the *po* to the lungs, the *yi* to the spleen, the *jing* to the kidneys, and the *shen* to the heart; yet now it is said:

Regarding the mutual roles of host and guest, how does this differ from such Daoist expressions as "the three flowers gathering," "the five qi ascending," "water and fire intersecting," or "metal and wood uniting"?

There are two meanings to this: first, those [Daoist] practices derive such results from performing such causes, whereas this sutra involves only the intensive investigation of one's own nature, wherein one attains it spontaneously without seeking it with a deliberate mind.
Regarding these two points: the former regards them as profound and mysterious, becoming so attached that they cannot let go;
whereas regarding the present sutra, he does not form a conception of it as sacred, and though it exists, he remains indifferent as if it were non-existent. This is the reason for their difference.
One observes without ceasing, suppresses, subdues, restrains, and transcends.
It is not necessary to apply suppression and so forth to the fourfold afflictions; rather, the meaning is self-evident when explained according to the sequence of the text.
First, "observation" refers to investigating the place of origin of the deluded mind. Second, "suppression" refers to [acting] at that very place of origin.
Yet one must suppress it; for although I firmly restrain it, it may not necessarily submit. Next, regarding "subduing" (dharana): whatever is restrained follows along in compliance.
Furthermore, fearing that after a temporary subjugation it might again leap up and act recklessly, "restraint" (dhāraṇā) serves as a further precaution to ensure it does not move.
Now, an analogy for the observer is like searching for a thief; one must first suppress [the mind].
Consider it as if one has already captured and subdued them, as if one has already compelled them to confess their guilt and restrained them, and furthermore imposed strict constraints upon them.
Because such successive punishments exceed all bounds, the wondrous clarity is driven to its limit and bursts forth in manifestation, causing empty space to take on the color of jewels.
This jeweled color of empty space is none other than the radiance of one’s own mind.
The mind detaches from the body and turns back to observe its own face; its coming and going are free and spontaneous, no longer subject to obstruction or hindrance.
This is roughly similar in intent to the "ejection of the spirit" (chushen) practiced by the family of transcendents (xianren), yet it is actually different.

In their case, one seeks it with the mind; here, one attains it without the mind. Theirs is called a "sublime function," whereas this does not constitute a "holy mind"—in these respects, it is the same as what was stated previously.
Furthermore, within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), when the body can momentarily emerge from obstructions, this is "emerging with intent.
Next, within the aggregate of form, when one sees afar and flies forth from extreme proximity, this is "gradual emergence.

Now, within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), when going and staying are free and there are no further obstructions, this is "sublime emergence. Again, within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), when the mind detaches from the body like a bird—
Those who have emerged from the cage are "wondrous beyond the wondrous," for they are able to ascend through the stages of sainthood and attain the body born of intention (*manomayakāya*).

That text contains the discourse on the "shadow spirit" (*chāyā-manas*) and the "sun spirit" (*sūrya-manas*); regarding these two states within the realm of form, the descriptions of the shadow spirit do not yet distinguish between the negative and positive aspects.

What is described as belonging to the shadow spirit is merely a semblance of the sun spirit; it does not reach the level of that true sun spirit, even though it still belongs to the category of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

As for this cultivation of the essence of awakening through the samādhi of right enlightenment, although its roots and sources differ, in sum it merely serves to break through the two aggregates of form and feeling;
that the three aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness remain unbroken is hardly something to marvel at.
Yet, to give rise to such marvelous thoughts and claim to have realized sainthood is surely the work of Māra manifesting itself—is it not fitting?

"Having no new realization before one, one returns to lose one's former abode"—this refers to when the demon of recollection arises because one has no new realization before oneself and thus loses the dwelling of the past. "New realization not yet attained, the old mind is already lost"—this refers to when the demon of anxiety arises because the new realization has not been obtained while the old mind has already perished.
What is the difference between these two? It is that while the objective conditions (*viṣaya*) are the same, the reasons for encountering them differ.

These are two different cases. In the first, one sees that both the preceding and succeeding states are liberated; desiring neither to maintain the former nor to turn toward the latter, one seeks a separate path from between them.
Consequently, day and night, one grasps at the mind with suspended thought and hanging concerns, and thus Māra enters.

In the second, one sees that both the preceding and succeeding states are liberated, yet one both desires to maintain the former and desires to retreat to the latter; thus, two thoughts arise in conflict.
Not knowing from where it comes, one's calculations are unsettled; thus, one wanders in anxiety and distress, allowing the demon of worry to enter.
Within this refined clarity, one perfectly awakens to the refined principle.
This means that after perfectly awakening to the refined principle within refined clarity, one subsequently attains the nature of empty luminosity within enlightened clarity.

These two instances of "awakening" (*wu*) refer to the realization that occurs when one breaks through the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and perceives the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
As the aggregate of sensation is about to become empty, one experiences a sense of refined unity and luminous clarity within the chest; this is merely awakening within the aggregate of sensation.

The remaining three aggregates are still as deluded and obscure as before, yet practitioners who reach this point claim they have attained awakening and that the great matter is finished. This is because they do not understand this.
From this ordinary body, one ascends through the sixty holy stages of a Bodhisattva to attain the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body).

Regarding these sixty holy stages, according to Mount Gu’s "Three Gradual Processes"—namely, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*), the Ten Faiths, the Ten Abidings, the Ten Practices, the Ten Transferences, the Four Additional Dwellings, and the Ten Grounds, including both the Equal and the Subtle—this enumeration appears to be the most stable and appropriate among all explanations. Furthermore, Mount Gu...

In the *Shanni jing* (Mount Mud Sutra), although the four characters "though not yet exhausted of outflows" (*weijin lou*) appear, it nevertheless judges the "mind-born body" (*yi-sheng-shen*) based on the stages of the seven, eight, and ten faiths.
However, the sutra states: "From this ordinary body, one ascends through the ranks of the sages to attain the mind-born body.

This precisely clarifies that for a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, they traverse the fruits of sagehood while remaining in their ordinary body. Moreover, "traversing" (*li*) refers to the successive stages and paths of the ranks of sagehood.
Master Lu said: "From this point on, one will certainly realize sainthood; it does not say that one is a saint right now. Even so, what obstacle is there?

According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, regarding the three types of mind-born bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), the first occurs in the third, fourth, and fifth stages; the second in the eighth stage; and the final one in the ninth stage.
Why must you doubt that this is too high and judge it to belong to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*)? It is, for example, like [the case of] Wuxing."

It is only at the eighth stage that the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is said to be correctly attained; yet this does not preclude the first stage from being called the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas—it is just like this.
One should not greedily seek mere conformity with these terms.

Within this aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), there is seeking skillfulness, seeking experience, seeking analytical discernment, seeking mystical resonance, seeking tranquility, seeking past lives, seeking spiritual power, seeking profound emptiness, and seeking longevity—these nine may not be urgent matters.

As for seeking "conformity" (*kaihe*), one desires to harmonize with the subtle principle; why, then, does this also give rise to demonic activity? In short, the illness lies in the very act of seeking.
It is merely the single character "one" and the single character "greed. The interpretation of the former virtuous masters was excellent, saying:

"When the workings of the mind are forgotten and there is tranquil illumination, the principle naturally meets in mystery. To seek a fit through a conceptualizing mind is already a deviation; from this, celestial māras gain their advantage. How profound these words are!
Nevertheless, if one forgets the workings of the mind while losing its illumination, one sinks into the stagnant waters of death; this, too, must be discerned.
Regarding the passage praising sexual conduct and not disparaging coarse behavior:
the text on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) states, "Praising sexual conduct and not disparaging coarse behavior. This is somewhat difficult to understand.

Some interpret it as praising that [person] for practicing sexual conduct without violating coarse behavior, let alone subtle behavior; thus, they take "coarse behavior" to belong to the side of virtue.
The meaning does not apply to the two uses of the character *huǐ* (毀). One is the *huǐ* of "slander" (*huìyù*), referring to reviling and calumny;

the other is the *huǐ* of "ruination" (*chéng huǐ*), referring to destruction and annihilation. The ancient gloss explains *huǐ* as *huī* (隳), which means to abandon or to annihilate—as in the case of Zhongni’s "abandoning the Three Bonds.
These two phrases refer to two distinct matters: first, regarding the dharma of lust, one instead adds praise to it.
Regarding the second [type of] lamentation: one settles the mind upon various coarse behaviors so as not to further destroy them.

"Coarse behaviors" refers to vulgar, base, and indecent matters that rank slightly below sexual desire; these include the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and other such matters belonging to the extreme side of evil.
○ Volume Ten: Eliminating Dreams and Fantasies.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, it is stated that only when the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty can one be said to be far removed from inverted dreams and fantasies; here, however, they are merely empty.
Why is it that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is also called the extinction of dreams? It is because while the terminology is the same, the depth of their meaning differs.
Now, speaking here specifically of this one aggregate, the Sūtra says: "During the day, the mind of perception is awake;

when asleep, it becomes various dreams. Therefore, when perception ceases, dreams cease. Because the dreams of perception have ceased, waking and sleeping are always one. As for that which is extinguished:

The *Benyin* (Root Aggregate) is merely the deluded thought of pervasive integration; the subtle thoughts of the *Xingyin* (Aggregate of Formations) and the minute thoughts of the *Shiyin* (Aggregate of Consciousness) have not yet been extinguished.

In that [other] sutra, it states that all five aggregates are empty; its mention of "perverse dreams and thoughts" does not stop at pervasive integration, but exhaustively includes the obscure and the minute.
Therefore, in this sutra, within the section on the aggregate of consciousness, it specifically says "perverse and minute."
The visualization of inverted characters perfectly accords with that sūtra’s account of inversion; this may serve as proof. Furthermore, according to the ultimate teaching of that sūtra:

for ordinary beings to conceive of the impermanent as permanent is an inverted dream-like delusion; for those of the Two Vehicles to conceive of the permanent as impermanent is an inverted dream-like delusion;
and for Bodhisattvas to cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices over many kalpas—[is likewise an inverted dream-like delusion].
If one does not enter the *Avataṃsaka*’s Dharma-door of Great Majestic Virtue, this is a delusion of dreams and fantasies;
it extends even to the flow of a single thought-moment of ignorance and the delusion of a single thought-moment of dreams and fantasies. How could this apply only to dreaming and sleep?
In this sutra, dreams are indeed real dreams. Why is this? Because when the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are correctly compared, they follow a fivefold sequence.
Because there are limits and boundaries.
It is like the subsiding and transformation of waves into clear water.
This clear water is called "great waves" in contrast to the waves; although the waves have ceased, the water has not yet come to rest.
The flowing seems as if it were not flowing; for a brief moment it is named "clear water," as stated later in the section on the delusive thoughts of the *vijñāna-skandha*:
"This stillness is not the True Suchness (*tathatā*); it is like a rushing torrent that appears tranquil because the flow is so rapid that it is not seen.
This is clear evidence that it is not a lack of flow. Nevertheless, it does not preclude calling it "clear water"; one simply values knowing this and must not give rise to arrogance. Thus it is said.
"Attainment" refers to attainment.

Regarding the post-mortem state of "neither [existence nor non-existence]," there arise inverted theories (and so forth), specifically the inverted theory of mind regarding the post-mortem state of "neither.
The Master of Wuxing states that of these two subsequent sections, the former section is "both" and the latter section is "neither"; thus, "both" implies that both are [existent].

Since the scripture states from beginning to end that both are "neither," how can you add "both are"? Furthermore, your own defense claims that the textual meaning is merely "provisionally posited" (*qie ji*) as "both.
However, it is extremely clear that the textual meaning is "both are neither"; why then insist on the explanation of it being "merely provisionally posited"?

This is because in the preceding section, by contrasting the three *skandhas* with the *saṃskāra-skandha*, it was explicitly stated that the three *skandhas* exist yet are not existent, while the *saṃskāra-skandha* is non-existent yet is not non-existent.
The conclusion states: "Regarding whether there is appearance or non-appearance after death," this is an abbreviated expression. If there is appearance, it is not non-existent;
if there is non-appearance, it is not existent. This is the first instance of "neither.

The subsequent section expands upon this, showing that from form, sensation, perception, and so forth, up to all phenomena in the world, they are all subject to change and decay—existent yet not existent, non-existent yet not non-existent.
Because one is able to fully comprehend and understand all within this, it is called "penetrating enlightenment. If it were not non-existent, the void would lose its voidness;
if it were not existent, the real would lose its reality. This is the second instance of "neither.

Looking toward the future limit in this way—dark, profound, vast, and boundless—one cannot say that the Way exists, nor can one say that the Way does not exist; one knows not where it goes. Therefore, it is said:
Because the future limit is dark and obscured, it cannot be described;
thus, "internally and externally, there is profound clarity" (and so forth). Internally and externally, there is transparent penetration.

Only when the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted can one speak of "luminous penetration. A profound clarity that is merely like still water is not yet true luminous penetration; only when it is transparently clear and penetrating, like beryl containing a precious moon, does it truly qualify as such.
One should therefore follow the various editions regarding both the internal and external [readings].

Regarding "union and separation" (*he-kai*), the ancient interpretation—that the sense organs are united without being partitioned and their objects are separated without being obstructed—does not yet fully satisfy the meaning. I now maintain that "union" and "separation" are antonyms, following the analogy of "totality and particularity" or "closing and opening.
Previously, although the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)...
As long as [ignorance] is not exhausted, the six gates remain fully present; one merely restrains them so that they do not run wild.
Now, when consciousness is exhausted, the source is depleted, the water dries up, the charcoal turns to ash, and the fire is extinguished.

Only then can the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) be dissolved, like ice that has already melted and vanished into the whole without substance or obstruction, or like a mirror that has been polished until it is brilliant and pure, free from all stains. Because the six gates have been thus dissolved...
Regarding "the union and separation that achieve union": although these sense-gates (indriya-mukha) are arranged as six distinct locations, they have never been anything other than one.
When [the mind] flows back toward its source, the brilliant clarity alone remains, with nothing else; it is like a bottle, a ring, a hairpin, and an armlet being made of the same gold.
This is what is meant by "union and separation. Although these six sense-gates are perfectly interfused, they each constitute a single [unit].
In all states, there is never anything that does not arise from the six [consciousnesses] as function from substance; thus, every gate is mutually connected without obstruction.

This is likened to a single piece of gold being fashioned into a jar, a ring, a hairpin, or an armlet. This is what is meant by "opening and closing. Since opening is sovereign, it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*).
However, since the subsequent section is still within the realm of consciousness, why is it said that it can cause the sense-faculties of one's own body to open and close?

In essence, "stopping" is called "convergence," while "opening" is not yet called "accomplishment. This still belongs to the realm of sudden convergence and sudden separation, or sudden opening and sudden partitioning;

how, then, could one immediately attain mutual functioning? Therefore, the fifth stage is merely the point within the mutual functioning of the six sense organs where one has already attained compliance.
"Compliance" means to move toward [the goal] without resistance; it is a designation for that which is about to be attained but is not yet attained.
"Extensively transforming [beings] with the seven treasures and increasing many precious ladies, allowing their minds to run wild"—this refers to those who give rise to superior resolve.
"The seven treasures" means extensively; "precious ladies" means many. This describes the ultimate exhaustion of luxury and the height of desire.

Furthermore, although it says within the text that these are those he himself has transformed, one should not allow the mind to run wild. How could one who has already exhausted the four aggregates (*skandhas*) further engage in such things?
Thus, regarding such coming and going, those who seek the Bodhisattva vehicle with a fervent mind for the benefit of others may indeed retain afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten their rebirth;
however, retaining afflictions to moisten rebirth is no small matter—it is something that only great beings of profound wisdom and vast vows can undertake with excellence.
Should one’s wisdom be somewhat deficient or one’s power of aspiration somewhat weak, once that tendency opens, its momentum cannot be checked.
At the beginning of indulgence, one may still have some sense of restraint, but by the end, one becomes so deeply immersed that one is unaware of it;
yet one still clings to this as a superior understanding, claiming to always be accompanied by desire while remaining untainted by its defilement.

This is like someone who has long been submerged in a latrine, where foul filth seeps in from all sides, yet when others cover their noses in disgust, he claims his body is in a sandalwood pavilion. Like Li Chi, is this not truly demonic?
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not achieve further progress.
The fifty kinds of Māras conclude with the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha—the fruits of Arhatship and Pratyekabuddhahood.
Why, then, are they also ranked among the Māras? Wuxing says that these two vehicles deviate from the Middle Way principle and give rise to heterodox views outside the realm.
To see that those who deviate from the Middle Way all fall into the biased realms of external heterodoxy is itself a form of heterodoxy;

therefore, they are equated with demons, yet in reality they differ from the aforementioned demons. As the Sūtra says: "When the karma induced by external paths and demonic influences is exhausted, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
In the case of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is simply said that they fail to progress further; this is because they have attained [a limited realization].

To be content with little and no longer seek advancement, remaining settled in a minor fruit—those who do not receive the Bodhisattva precepts according to the Brahmajāla Sūtra are all termed those of "evil habit," and those who study the Two Vehicles are all termed "perverse. The meaning is likewise this:
they are like those who share the same root but reach different destinations.
"If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted" (and so forth), one enters the Tathāgata’s wondrous ocean of adornment.
The Sūtra states: "If the aggregate of consciousness is exhausted, then your present sense faculties will function interchangeably;

from this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom. In this way, you transcend the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and orientation, proceeding until you reach Equal Enlightenment and enter [the ultimate state]."
"The Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornments perfects Bodhi and returns to non-attainment"—this is the ultimate expression.

Regarding the two characters "ni" (mud) and "ru" (enter) from Mount Gu, they assign the seventh stage of faith to this position. I, however, believe the intent of the Sūtra refers to the Vajra-dry-wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*).
From where does one enter? One enters from within these six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). It is by entering directly through these that one enters; it is not a gradual process.
Next is the gradual entry. These few words fully reveal the direct pointing of the Chan school;

as it is said, "Simply exhaust the ordinary mind, and there is no separate 'sage-understanding,'" and again, "In one leap, enter directly into the stage of the Tathāgata"—this is precisely that meaning.

This differs from the previous description of the sixty stages of sagehood when the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling-aggregate) is exhausted; the former speaks of "passing through," while this speaks of "entering."
To look upward from below is called "traversing" (*li*), and for the body to have already arrived is called "entering" (*ru*).
When Bodhi is perfected, it appears as if there were something attained; therefore, it is immediately followed by "returning to non-attainment. As for Bodhi: [it is the state of awakening].
Originally there was never any loss; how can one now speak of attaining Bodhi? Originally there was never any deficiency;

how can one now speak of perfecting Bodhi? Originally there is no place; where would one wish to return? To return to nothingness and find nothing to obtain—this is what is called true attainment, true return, and true perfection.
Knowing that which arises from delusion, one explains the causes and conditions of delusion (and so forth), [realizing they] originally do not exist at all.
As stated above, even the nature of that empty space is still a real delusion arising through causes and conditions of its own accord;

how could it not be delusory? The reason for this is that because one knows all phenomena arise entirely from delusion, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion within the midst of delusion.

If this delusion existed inherently, then its causes and conditions would also exist; yet if delusion is fundamentally non-existent, then those causes and conditions are themselves fundamentally non-existent.

Since causes and conditions are merely provisional designations, how much more so is it the case that one who does not understand that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions fails to find their arising when sought, and instead pushes the matter aside as being "natural"? This only serves to further increase their false conceptualizations.
If your mind is not characterized by thought, you will be unable to come into the midst of thought to transmit the mandate.

The *He lun* (Treatise on Concordance), in its supplementary notes, states: "The Confucianist speaks of 'knowing the mandate,' the Daoist speaks of 'returning to the mandate,' and the Buddhist speaks of 'transmitting the mandate.
The intent [of these terms] is that their meanings are identical; yet these three are in fact distinct, and one must examine this carefully. The Master said: "To not know..."
Regarding the statement, "Destiny cannot be made by man to become a gentleman," and further, "Life and death are matters of destiny," Mencius said:

"One who knows destiny does not stand beneath a crumbling wall. Thus, what is meant by "destiny" in these cases refers to poverty or prosperity, and early or late death; it is not the "destiny" spoken of today [in the sense of fatalism].
If one says, "Exhausting principle and exhausting nature until reaching destiny," then this destiny is the original source of nature—the Heaven that is profoundly silent and unceasing.

Life-force (*jīva*) is also not what is meant by "life" (*ming*) here. Some Daoist schools take the navel wheel (*cakra*) to be the "vitality-root" (*ming-di*), or the *dantian* to be the "palace of life" (*ming-gong*).
Alternatively, when speaking in contrast to the nature (*xing*), they hold that the original spirit (*yuan-shen*) is the nature and the original breath (*yuan-qi*) is the life-force;

yet this too is not what is meant by "life" here. What is meant by "life" here is that the three things—consciousness (*vijñāna*), warmth (*uṣman*), and breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*)—mutually depend upon one another to constitute life.
The breath depends on warmth, and warmth depends on consciousness (*vijñāna*). Once the breath ceases, warmth is extinguished; once warmth is extinguished, consciousness departs.
Consciousness is the source of warmth and the root of the breath; it is that by which life is established. To speak exhaustively, there are three;
to speak concisely, there is one—consciousness encompasses them all. Therefore, this sutra says: "Even if your physical form dissolves and the radiance of your life-force passes away, as for life..."
It is said that this refers to what is called "radiant, correct consciousness" (*vijñāna*). The movement of this consciousness constitutes "perception" (*saṃjñā*);

because my mind is attached to perception, at the moment of rebirth, I follow the perception of the parents who are to give birth to me. By uniting my perception with their perception, these two perceptions converge, and through this, I enter the womb.
Thus, the life-force of the preceding *skandha* (aggregates) is transformed into the life-force of the succeeding *skandha*. It is like...
Because succession continues without interruption, it is called the "transmission of life. If the mind were not consciousness, their categories would differ and their natures would be distinct;
how then could there be the principle of water transmitting fire, fire transmitting water, a cow transmitting a horse, or a horse transmitting a cow?
Therefore, when deluded thoughts are exhausted, birth and death are exhausted.
"Deeply entering the profound stillness, one returns to the limit of consciousness.
The first character "profound" (*zhàn*) refers to the practice of not allowing [the mind] to flow out or become dissipated; the second character "profound" refers to the essence of profound clarity.

This is precisely the meaning of what was stated previously: "using profound stillness to revolve back its falsity," "returning the flow to restore the oneness," and "subduing it so it returns to the original truth."
In this way, this stillness is not true suchness; it is like the appearance of tranquility in a rushing torrent—it is merely the boundary and limit of the eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, as previously described in the section on the *xing-yin* (form-sky), when waves subside and transform into clear water, this water is not the ultimate reality;

it is precisely this very stillness. This stillness, when joined with [the stillness of] the *ālaya-vijñāna*, is the realm of consciousness, wherein the practitioner briefly attains a sense of light ease.
If one who has merely attained the Way [still feels this way], how much more so for one who has reached this point where the four aggregates have already ceased and only consciousness remains?

How could they not feel a sense of exhilaration, thinking to themselves that they have realized *nirvāṇa*? Yet how could they know that this profound stillness is precisely the subtle root of birth and death?

Because it is not yet exhausted, darkness grows and nourishes itself in secret; from the minute it becomes manifest, and from the subtle it becomes massive. Based on these old habits, one will once again become an ant.
If mosquitoes and gnats still arise in your head, you must clarify it further and further, purify it again and again;

only when it is like a ten-thousand-fathom clear pool where water and sky are one color will this be the news of having arrived home. To take a little as sufficient—how can that be? How could it ever be so?
"Principle is realized suddenly, and with realization it is simultaneously extinguished; phenomena are not suddenly eliminated, for they are exhausted through gradual stages.

This refers to what is called "sudden enlightenment followed by gradual cultivation" in the Chan school. Of the four lines and two meanings, the first line of each pair indicates the principle, while the second line further clarifies it.
It states that regarding the extinction of these five aggregates (*skandhas*), there are aspects that can be realized suddenly and those that cannot.
That which can be sudden is principle (*li*). For principle has no dual nature;

it is only because people are deluded regarding its source that they must rely on this single awakening to merge and exhaust all [delusions] until nothing remains. It is like holding a torch into a dark room:

once it is bright, everything becomes bright; how could there be any sequence? That which cannot be sudden is phenomena (*shi*). For phenomena are myriad and diverse, and their conditions are difficult to overcome.
Because they are practiced concurrently, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep in successive stages until all is exhausted. It is like washing and refining a soiled garment:

it becomes gradually bright and clean; how could it be cleansed all at once? However, the principle of sudden enlightenment is the principle inherent in phenomena (*dharma*), not the principle of the "emptiness of annihilation" of the Two Vehicles.
The process of gradual elimination is the phenomenon inherent in the principle; it is not the "attachment to existence" of ordinary beings.
This is a matter of practice: sudden awakening is like ice becoming water, while gradual elimination is like water becoming ice; how could they be two distinct things?
Therefore, although Sudhana had already resolved his mind upon supreme bodhicitta, he nonetheless had to visit fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Guishan said that even if a practitioner attains sudden awakening to their own nature through conditions, there still remains a lack of... [the text here is incomplete].
That initial habitual tendencies cannot be purified instantaneously—requiring both sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation—is the doctrine of the sudden and the gradual.
These sixteen characters are the definitive instruction transmitted by the thousand Buddhas and the grand standard that shall never change for ten thousand generations;
those who study this path should devote their whole hearts to them.
Knowing that there is *nirvāṇa*, one does not cling to the three realms.
There are two senses of "knowing": the first is the knowledge of hearing and seeing. Hearing it taught that *nirvāṇa* is the place of refuge, one pursues it in every thought;
how could one then cling to the three realms? It is like a destitute son who, knowing he has a hometown, no longer craves [his current state].
The first [verse] refers to being attached to a foreign land and desiring to dwell there for a long time. The second, "the one who knows," refers to the knowledge of awakening.
Having already awakened to the true bliss of Nirvana residing within oneself, why would one be attached to the three realms? It is like a destitute son who has returned to his native home;
how could he ever again yearn for a foreign land and wish to dwell there? Nowadays, people merely recite the passage on the three realms as a burning house.
Yet the mind is truly and earnestly attached to them, unable to let go, because it does not know that there is nirvana.
It does not worry about not escaping the triple world; its only worry is not knowing nirvana. How great is the significance of knowing it!
One is able, with a single thought, to reveal and teach this Dharma-gate to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa.

As the Sūtra says: "The merit of being able to reveal and teach this Dharma-gate to those who have not yet studied—such that those on the verge of entering the Avīci Hell immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī—is such that even the merit of making offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are sands in the Ganges would not equal even a small fraction of it. This refers to understanding and realization.
Upon seeing this text, the wild current gave rise to great conceit and ceased his diligent practice;
how could he have known that a single word of the Buddha inherently possesses both the benefit of self and the benefit of others?

Now he only knows to use this Dharma-gate to instruct those who have not yet studied, yet he never knew to use this Dharma-gate to instruct his own lack of learning—how can his ignorance reach such an extreme!
Thus, appended to the various sutras: The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra).
Regarding "Prajñā-citta" (the Heart of Wisdom):
Xianshou’s Commentary states that "prajñā" is the dharma and "citta" is a metaphor; one interpretation holds it is not a metaphor, stating it is the "mind of prajñā-wisdom.
Each has its own intent. Now, following Xianshou’s excellent reasoning, since the mind is the sovereign of the hundred physical constituents, and this sutra...
Because this brief text encapsulates the complete meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* through the presence of mental images (*citta-nimitta*),
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—
according to the translation by Shi Hu, this was spoken by the Great Being— should have the word "said" (*uvāca*) following "Bodhisattva"; however, it is currently [omitted].
The Buddha taught this as being so; it can be verified by both the translations of Master Kumārajīva and Master Xuanzang.
These are the characteristics of the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Emptiness is fundamentally without characteristics, yet because one wishes for people to recognize emptiness, its characteristics are specifically set forth within that which is without characteristics, stating that "there is no... [existence].

That which arises and ceases, is defiled and pure, increases and decreases, is the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Since the characteristic of emptiness is thus, the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*) becomes even more manifest. *Gate*.
The Commentary previously stated that "divine mantras are secret and not translated," yet subsequently remarked that they may nonetheless be forcibly translated. It provides the reason:
"In Sanskrit, *gate* means 'going' or 'crossing over' in Chinese. This is because the two syllables *ga-te* form the Sanskrit term, and its meaning is "to go" or "to cross over";
it does not mean that the character *qu* (go) is used to translate *ga*, nor that *ga* refers to "removing" (*qu*) the obstacles of delusion. Since this is already called a "forced" translation...
To "strive" is a term for being compelled by necessity rather than acting spontaneously; how could it compare to simply ceasing?
*The Complete Enlightenment Sutra* states:
"Knowing these are but flowers in the sky, there is no further transmigration, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death... (and so forth).
That cognizer is like space; that which knows space is itself the appearance of a flower in the sky, and its nature of non-cognition cannot be said not to exist.
In the commentary, "knowing" refers to the two phrases concerning the dharma of no birth-and-death, and "not knowing" refers to the two phrases concerning the lack of escape from saṃsāra.

The two phrases "the person knows that" negate through contemplative wisdom the knowledge of emptiness; the two phrases "the mind is extinguished" negate even the negating mind, so that it is not two. These two phrases block and sever [delusion];
their teaching is exceedingly refined and cannot be altered for ten thousand ages. One interpretation states:

"Knowing this to be a flower in the sky, one is immediately liberated from saṃsāra. What persons or dharmas could there be? That which is aware and cognizant is my true nature, just like empty space. To give rise to a thought...
To say that knowing emptiness is itself like a flower in the sky, and thus to speak as one pleases, may seem convenient; however, this must be examined in light of the scriptural text.

The text first states, "knowing these are flowers in the sky," next says, "that which knows and perceives," then says, "knowing empty space," and finally says, "nor can it be said that there is no nature of knowing and perceiving.
It concludes again by stating, "within the Tathāgatagarbha."

Because of a lack of understanding and insight, one must read it by fusing and penetrating the five characters for "knowledge" (知) throughout the preceding and following sections; only then will one realize that this commentary is not composed with superficiality.
All manner of acceptance and rejection are nothing but saṃsāra.
Guifeng [Zongmi] took delight in that *Sukhāvatī* as the means for "taking" (*upādāna*) and felt aversion toward this *Sahā* world as the means for "rejecting" (*pratyāga*).
This was intended for those of superior faculties to dispel their attachments; yet those who clung to his words instead gave rise to doubts and obstructions, becoming unwilling to seek rebirth there.

Nowadays, people rely solely on Guifeng’s brief commentary and have not seen the interpretations of other masters. Taishui [Zongxiao] says: "The Sūtra speaks of 'beginning,' 'end,' and so forth, citing worldly phenomena."

such a thing is also not [the Middle]. Therefore, there is the "mere Middle" and the "not-mere Middle. "Mere" means solitary. When the Middle is solitary, the extremes are not the Middle.

If it is "not-mere," then there are no extremes, and thus it is not the Middle. As the former masters said: "Whatever is brought forth is not not [the Way]," and they also said: "Great merit and virtue."
It is said that a person may take a stone and fashion it into a jewel; it is further said that every color and every fragrance is none other than the Middle Way;

and it is also said that even a cough, a spittle, or a swinging of the arms is not anything other than the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West—this is what is meant by "observing the middle within the extremes.

Since the relationship between phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*) can be understood through these examples, how clear, simple, straightforward, and direct this is! It is the very nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
If one is naturally free from artificial fabrication, is it not fitting to call this "straightforwardness"?

Conversely, to look back with such constraint—first abandoning extremes to seek the middle, then discarding phenomena to pursue principle—is merely to see a process of forced synthesis and compromise;
it is circuitous, indirect, and emerges from fabrication rather than nature. Is it not fitting to call this "deviousness"? How great!
This sutra is the Buddha’s final exhortation; its words are near while its meaning is far-reaching, and it must not be treated with negligence.
△ *The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere."
One should also give rise to the mind without abiding; one should not give rise to the mind with abiding. That which arises without abiding is the pure mind.
If one suspects that the mind is fundamentally unarisen and thus cannot be said to arise, consider the following text, which states:
"One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere," and further, "One should not abide in form when giving rise to the mind. The former [passage] says "should," and the latter...
The statement "should not dwell" is repeated for clarification: that which arises from non-dwelling is that arising is itself non-arising.
Regarding the "four-line verse" and so forth, there are various interpretations of these four lines;
however, Zhongfeng maintains that wherever the sutra mentions a "four-line verse," it must necessarily be preceded by [the phrase]: "If one can uphold even a single four-line verse..."
Regarding the phrase "even down to a single word," the inclusion of the word "etc.

(*ādi*) implies that within this sutra, upholding even one line, two lines, or even four lines, as well as ten, a hundred, or a thousand lines and so forth, is what is most appropriate. This is especially clear when considering the subsequent passage which states:
"Wherever this sutra is expounded, even if it be but a single four-line verse," where the word "even" (*yāvat*) makes the meaning even more explicit.
If a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the Buddha-lands," they would not be called a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not adorn the Buddha-lands; how then could the Bhikṣu Dharmākara have adorned the Land of Ultimate Bliss with his forty-eight vows?
There are two meanings to this: first, because the gates are different, Prajñāpāramitā is the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). It is not...
To receive the Dharma-treasury of a single atom is to not abandon a single dharma within the gateway of the Buddha’s work.

Second, because emptiness and existence are non-dual, the Sūtra says: "Although one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates pure lands to teach and transform all sentient beings.
Therefore, those who resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding dharmas.
If it were said that a bodhisattva who makes such a statement as "I do not adorn buddha-fields" would not be called a bodhisattva,
this would also be correct; likewise, while he brings about the parinirvāṇa of boundless sentient beings, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa—
thus, though he adorns them all day long, he has never adorned them.
"In this way, in this manner, one contemplates the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks" (and so forth)... "Regarding phenomena, I do not speak of a mark of annihilation.
The Buddha-body is not a [physical] mark; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Subhūti, having already understood this...

Wu-jin asks a question no different from the previous one, yet his answer seems, on the contrary, to be confused. He then asks: "What is meant by 'one who can contemplate the Tathāgata through mutual observation'?
There are two ancient interpretations. The Tiantai school considers this [first] answer to be a "deviant answer" (邪答) and the subsequent answer to be the "intentional understanding" (領會意).

They say that while the sentiments of the time held the former to be so, my own interpretation is not thus; rather, it is the sentiments of the time that have misapprehended the first answer as deviant, while regarding the subsequent answer as correct.
Subhūti himself understood this as an acknowledgment; however, while the question remained the same, the answer was different, and the meaning was not yet clear.

Worthy Leader [Yuanxiao], relying on the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, maintained that the previous statement—that one cannot see [the Buddha] by means of marks—refers to awakening to the form-body (*rūpakāya*), whereas the present statement—that one can see him by means of marks—still refers to being deluded regarding the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
This is because Subhūti already knew that the form-body flows forth from the dharma-body, and thus the form-body is itself the dharma-body.
One may observe the Dharma-body as being like a sprout emerging from its root; just as one can observe the root through the sprout, it is said:

"In this way, in this way. When [Subhūti] observed the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, the Buddha questioned him: "Since the marks of a Wheel-turning King are no different from those of a Buddha, could he not be the Tathāgata?
Subhūti then understood the Buddha’s intention, realizing that the Buddha’s marks arise from the Dharma-body.
Although the marks of a Wheel-Turning King are identical to those of a Buddha, they arise from merit; how then can one perceive the Tathāgata through the thirty-two marks?
The Buddha granted this, yet he further feared that [the interlocutor] might sink into the view of signlessness (*animitta*), failing to realize that form is itself emptiness.
Therefore, he said again: "Do not entertain such thoughts, for the Tathāgata does not attain bodhi by means of marks," and so on, up to: "One should generate the thought of bodhi..."

Regarding those who grasp at the mind, the Buddha does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena, for fear that they might become attached to characteristics; he then dispels characteristics.
Fearing that they might become attached to emptiness, he then dispels emptiness. This continues until both form and emptiness are simultaneously extinguished and yet simultaneously preserved.
When both preservation and extinction are forgotten, and there is nothing further to be dispelled, this is the true emptiness of Prajñā.

"According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
One must not, upon encountering this teaching that the mind is pure and the land is pure, seek to negate the existence of the Pure Land; for according to principle, it is precisely...
The mind is itself the land; when the mind is pure, it is called the purity of the land. Why then need one further aspire for rebirth there?

According to the facts, the character "follow" (隨) at the top [of the phrase] corresponds to the cause, while the character "follow" (隨) at the bottom corresponds to the effect. When the mind follows purity, the land thereby becomes pure;
when the mind follows defilement, the land thereby becomes defiled. In the following passage, Śāriputra had this thought: "The World-Honored One, for the sake of Bodhi..."
If at that time the mind were not pure, how could this Buddha-land be so impure? Thus one knows that purity of mind is the cause and purity of the land is the result;
it is clear, therefore, that there must be a pure land.

Rather, it means that when not a single thought arises, all practices are spontaneously complete; for one does not respond to objects with the mind, but responds to objects with the physical form.
Therefore, Master Sengzhao said: "While the mind and intellect are eternally extinguished, the physical form reaches the eight extremities.
This means that while externally it manifests more fully, internally it becomes increasingly tranquil. Only Śāriputra!
The character "wei" (唯) cannot be marked with the third tone; if it were so marked, its pronunciation would have to be "wěi," like the sound of assent.

If it is not so marked, its pronunciation remains as that of the original character, serving as a particle of exhortation. When another person speaks, one responds here with "wei" (唯) as an expression of assent.
Now, since Śāriputra has said nothing, what did Vimalakīrti hear that he assented?

some say that the scripture lists these nine grades as a teaching specifically intended to enable those of both dull and sharp faculties to attain rebirth through the practice of visualization (*vipaśyanā*).

Rebirth [in the Pure Land] is an easy path; yet, Master Zhili’s commentary on this sutra emphasizes the "single mind" and the "threefold contemplation" so profoundly and mysteriously that it instead becomes a difficult path to practice.

At first, I also thought so, but now I realize that the original title of that commentary was *Miaozong* (The Wondrous Pivot), intended for all who seek rebirth to give rise to the supreme aspiration.
The mind conforms to the Tathāgata; this mind is the Buddha, and this is the fundamental intent of "this mind creates the Buddha.

These three matters are called "pure karma.

What is the reason for this? It is because there are many gateways to rebirth; one need not necessarily cultivate all sixteen contemplations to be born [in the Pure Land]. All the six perfections and myriad practices are likewise [gateways].

One may dedicate these merits toward the Western Land; however, because these sixteen contemplations serve as the most essential cause, the Buddha has painstakingly revealed them to universally deliver all sentient beings.

Furthermore, when one brings phenomena back to their underlying principle, the three types of merit and so forth all enter into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is itself the wondrous contemplation.
△ In the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*,
it is stated that Avalokiteśvara succeeds Amitābha upon his parinirvāṇa. Since there is indeed such a parinirvāṇa, how [can he succeed]?
To attain an immeasurable lifespan has two meanings: first, Amitābha is inherently the immeasurable within the measurable;
although his lifespan has a measure, because no one can know the limit of that measure, it is both measurable and immeasurable.
